spheres.title: SCHONHAGE-STRASSEN
spheres.credit: A genuine JOINT credit (eponym correct): Arnold Schonhage & Volker Strassen, one 1971 paper 'Schnelle Multiplikation grosser Zahlen'. But it is NOT the first fast (sub-quadratic) multiply - that is Karatsuba (1962, dart 041); Schonhage-Strassen is the first NEAR-LINEAR method O(n log n log log n). It uses a Number-Theoretic Transform (exact integer FFT over rings Z/(2^(2^m)+1), Fermat numbers), NOT a floating-point complex FFT. The FFT it relies on is Cooley-Tukey 1965 (Gauss had it ~1805, unpublished); J. M. Pollard independently gave the NTT the SAME year (1971) and is usually omitted
spheres.source: Schonhage & Strassen, Computing 7:281-292, 1971; Karatsuba & Ofman 1962 (dart 041); Cooley & Tukey 1965; Pollard, Math. Comp. 25:365-374, 1971 (NTT); Furer 2007; Harvey & van der Hoeven, Annals of Math 193, 2021 (O(n log n))
spheres.i13_recommend: the LIT part RUNS on the corpus's bignum today: schoolbook O(n^2) and Karatsuba O(n^1.585) (dart 041) already multiply, and the worked example - digit convolution [5,16,34,60,61,52,32] with carry to 7,006,652 - is just the schoolbook convolution written out, so it runs directly (verified 1234 x 5678 = 7,006,652). The FRONTIER that hits a wall is the FFT/NTT acceleration (dart 059): a number-theoretic transform needs a modular FFT with roots of unity, expressible over bignum but a real build, and it only OVERTAKES Karatsuba/Toom-Cook at thousands of digits (the crossover). It closes the near-linear-multiplication lineage the corpus already runs: Karatsuba (041), the FFT (059), bignum.
spheres.blurb: To multiply two enormous integers, treat their digits as a signal: the product's digits are the CONVOLUTION of the two digit lists, and a Fast Fourier Transform computes a convolution in O(n log n) instead of O(n^2). Schonhage and Strassen's key trick (1971) was to run the FFT not over floating-point complex numbers (round-off error) but over the ring of integers modulo a Fermat number 2^(2^m)+1 - a Number-Theoretic Transform where 2 is a convenient root of unity, so every step is exact integer arithmetic - giving O(n log n log log n) and the asymptotic crown from 1971 to 2007. The eponym is a genuine joint credit (one paper, two authors), but two corrections: it is NOT the first fast multiply - Karatsuba broke O(n^2) first in 1962 (dart 041), and Schonhage-Strassen is the first NEAR-LINEAR method, not the first fast one - and J. M. Pollard independently published the same number-theoretic transform the same year (1971), usually left off the credit line. The FFT it leans on is Cooley-Tukey 1965 (and Gauss had the FFT around 1805, unpublished, so crediting them as inventors understates its prehistory). Furer (2007) finally beat it asymptotically, and Harvey & van der Hoeven reached O(n log n) in 2019/2021 - exactly the bound Schonhage and Strassen conjectured back in 1971. In real I-13 the LIT part runs on bignum (schoolbook + Karatsuba already multiply; verified 1234 x 5678 = 7,006,652 via the digit convolution an FFT accelerates); the FFT/NTT is the frontier, and it only overtakes Karatsuba past thousands of digits - superseded in theory (galactic algorithms), still the practical method for enormous integers (GMP).

spheres.title: THE THOMAS ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: 'Thomas algorithm' is a LATER-attached label, not a self-claim: the name was coined by David M. Young, and per W. F. Ames the method was independently discovered several times - it is simply Gaussian elimination on a tridiagonal matrix. Llewellyn H. Thomas never PUBLISHED it; the eponymous source is an UNPUBLISHED 1949 Watson Scientific Computing Laboratory internal report at Columbia, titled 'Elliptic Problems in Linear DIFFERENCE Equations over a Network' (frequently mis-titled 'Differential'). Thomas is far more famous for the Thomas-Fermi atom model and the hydrogen fine structure
spheres.source: L. H. Thomas 1949 (unpublished Columbia Watson Lab report); name coined by David M. Young (per W. F. Ames / Cleve Moler NA-Digest)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - and it is a POSTER CHILD for sidestepping PS-004 (the 2-D-array want). A tridiagonal A is only three diagonals, so it is held as three separate 1-D f64 arrays - sub-diagonal a[], diagonal b[], super-diagonal c[] - plus the rhs d[]; no 2-D array is ever allocated, so the missing-2-D-array limitation never bites. Every operation in both sweeps is a plain f64 multiply / subtract / divide (m = b[i] - a[i]*cprime[i-1]; cprime[i] = c[i]/m; dprime[i] = (d[i]-a[i]*dprime[i-1])/m; then back-substitute), verified x = [3,5,4] for a 3x3 system. O(n) time and space. It is Gauss / Householder (089) narrowed to a band - where a general solve wants a matrix (PS-004), the tridiagonal case runs on the arrays the corpus already has.
spheres.blurb: When a linear system is TRIDIAGONAL - only the main diagonal and its two neighbours are nonzero, as in every 1-D heat, spline, or finite-difference problem - you do not need full Gaussian elimination: one forward-elimination sweep and one back-substitution solve it in O(n). It is Gauss specialised, and it is named for a man who never published it. 'Thomas algorithm' is a later label coined by David M. Young; Llewellyn H. Thomas wrote the method in an UNPUBLISHED 1949 Columbia Watson Lab internal report (titled 'Elliptic Problems in Linear DIFFERENCE Equations over a Network', commonly mis-titled 'Differential') and never claimed it, and per W. F. Ames it was independently discovered several times - it is simply Gaussian elimination on a tridiagonal matrix. Without pivoting it can be unstable, but for diagonally dominant systems (the usual case) it is exact and stable; and Thomas himself is far more famous for the Thomas-Fermi atom model and computing the hydrogen fine structure - the tridiagonal solver was a footnote. In real I-13 it is nothing new and a poster child for sidestepping the PS-004 2-D-array want: hold the three diagonals as three separate 1-D f64 arrays (plus the rhs), so no 2-D array is ever needed, and every step is f64 multiply/subtract/divide (verified x = [3,5,4]) - Gauss narrowed to a band, running on the arrays the corpus already has.
spheres.kicker: dart 111 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: GIBBS SAMPLING
spheres.credit: Josiah Willard Gibbs (1839-1903) had NOTHING to do with the algorithm and never saw a computer - it is named after the Gibbs (Boltzmann-Gibbs) DISTRIBUTION that Stuart & Donald Geman (biological BROTHERS) happened to sample when they coined the name in 1984 (image restoration). 1984 is when the NAME was coined, not when the mechanism was invented: physicists had the identical 'heat bath' algorithm earlier - Roy Glauber's 1963 single-site heat-bath updating of the Ising model. Gelfand & Smith (1990) brought it to mainstream Bayesian statistics
spheres.source: S. Geman & D. Geman, IEEE PAMI 1984 (coined the name); R. Glauber 1963 (heat-bath, the same algorithm); Gelfand & Smith 1990 (Bayesian mainstream); J. W. Gibbs (the distribution)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the stdlib seeded LCG emits uniforms; the full conditionals sit in an f64 array; each coordinate update is a single comparison u < P; coordinates cycle in fixed order; running means accumulate. Under a fixed seed the whole trace is reproducible, and the empirical marginals converge to the truth (verified LCG seed 112, 3000 sweeps: E[X] -> 0.387, E[Y] -> 0.487, targets 0.40 / 0.50). It is Metropolis-Hastings (dart 031) with acceptance always 1 (proposing from the full conditional gives ratio 1). Like rejection sampling (107), determinism-under-seed is the feature - the 'random' algorithm is exactly reproducible, which a hash-sealed corpus wants.
spheres.blurb: To sample a hard joint distribution, Gibbs sampling does the easy thing repeatedly: hold all variables but one fixed, draw that one from its full CONDITIONAL distribution, move to the next, and cycle; even from a bad start the chain converges to the true joint, so empirical frequencies match it. It powers Bayesian inference and image models - and it is named for Josiah Willard Gibbs (1839-1903), who died decades before any computer and had nothing to do with it: the name honours the Gibbs (Boltzmann-Gibbs) DISTRIBUTION that Stuart and Donald Geman (biological brothers) sampled when they coined 'Gibbs sampling' in 1984 for image restoration. And 1984 is only when the NAME appeared - physicists had the identical 'heat bath' algorithm 21 years earlier in Roy Glauber's 1963 single-site updating of the Ising model, and Gelfand and Smith (1990) later brought it to mainstream Bayesian statistics. It is a special case of Metropolis-Hastings (dart 031) where every proposal is accepted, because the conditional does the work. In real I-13 it is nothing new: the seeded LCG emits uniforms, the conditionals sit in an f64 array, each update is one comparison u < P, and running means accumulate (verified seed 112, 3000 sweeps -> E[X] 0.387, E[Y] 0.487, converging to 0.40/0.50, reproducible bit-for-bit under the seed).
spheres.kicker: dart 112 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: TWO-WAY STRING MATCHING
spheres.credit: The eponym is RIGHT for the algorithm (Crochemore & Perrin, JACM 38(3):651-675, 1991) but the Critical Factorization Theorem it runs on is older (Cesari & Vincent, sharpened by Jean-Pierre Duval). Its standard-library home is memmem / strstr in glibc, musl, and newlib - NOT libc++ std::string::find, which in both libc++ and libstdc++ is a NAIVE O(n*m) two-pointer scan. It achieves linear time with CONSTANT extra space (no O(m) precomputed table, unlike KMP-063 and Boyer-Moore-061)
spheres.source: Crochemore & Perrin, J. ACM 38(3):651-675, 1991; Critical Factorization Theorem: Cesari & Vincent, sharpened by J.-P. Duval; glibc/musl/newlib memmem & strstr implementations
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - encode text and pattern as f64 arrays of code points; the two directional scans (compare the right part left-to-right, the left part right-to-left) are index comparisons over those arrays; the critical position and the shift amount are integer arithmetic held in a fixed handful of scalars (critical position, period, two cursors). Crucially it needs NO auxiliary array - the O(1)-extra-space property survives directly on i13's bounded arrays (verified match at index 5 for pattern GCAGAGAG in the text, period 7). The standing STRING want (Boyer-Moore-061, KMP-063, BWT-065, LZ78-102) is the only shadow; the matching itself needs nothing more.
spheres.blurb: Two-Way string matching finds a pattern in a text in LINEAR time and - unlike KMP or Boyer-Moore - with CONSTANT extra space (no precomputed table the size of the pattern): it factors the pattern at a 'critical position' into a left part u and right part v (from the pattern's maximal suffixes) and scans both directions, using the pattern's own period to decide each shift with only a handful of integer variables. It is the string search compiled into glibc, musl, and newlib's memmem and strstr - the matcher your programs actually call (NOT libc++ std::string::find, which is a naive O(n*m) scan). The eponym is correct for the algorithm (Crochemore & Perrin, J. ACM 38(3):651-675, 1991), but the Critical Factorization Theorem it stands on is older - Cesari and Vincent, sharpened by Jean-Pierre Duval. Against KMP (dart 063) and Boyer-Moore (dart 061), which precompute O(m)-size tables, Two-Way's O(1) extra space is exactly why C libraries chose it. In real I-13 it is nothing new: encode text and pattern as f64 code-point arrays, the two directional scans are index comparisons, and the critical position, period, and shift are integer arithmetic in a fixed handful of scalars - needing NO auxiliary array (verified match at index 5, period 7), so the O(1)-space property survives directly on the bounded arrays.
spheres.kicker: dart 113 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: JOHNSON'S ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: The eponym is Donald Bruce Johnson (1933-1994, PhD Cornell 1973 under David Gries, founding chair of the Dartmouth College CS department) - NOT David S. Johnson of the 'Garey & Johnson' NP-completeness fame. And the reweighting/node-potential trick (making reduced edge costs w + h(u) - h(v) non-negative) is NOT Johnson's invention - node potentials come from min-cost-flow theory (Edmonds-Karp era); Johnson's contribution is USING them for all-pairs shortest paths
spheres.source: D. B. Johnson, 'Efficient algorithms for shortest paths in sparse networks', J. ACM 24(1):1-13, 1977; node potentials from min-cost-flow (Edmonds-Karp era); Bellman-Ford (dart 046) + Dijkstra (dart 055)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - it LITERALLY composes two darts the corpus already runs. Add a virtual source with zero-weight edges to every vertex (just a longer edge list, no new primitive) and run BELLMAN-FORD (dart 046) ONCE, yielding potentials h[] as a 1-D f64 array (the same pass detects a negative cycle and aborts for free); reweight every edge to w' = w + h(u) - h(v) - pure f64 arithmetic, all edges become >= 0; then run DIJKSTRA (dart 055) from each vertex over the reweighted graph and undo the shift (verified A->C = -3 via B on a graph with a negative edge). The distance output is a 2-D matrix (PS-004). A textbook example of the campaign's thesis: two landed features compound into a new capability with no new primitive, like Pollard p-1 (083) reusing modexp + gcd.
spheres.blurb: Johnson's algorithm computes all-pairs shortest paths on a SPARSE graph that may have negative edges - too sparse for Floyd-Warshall's n^3, but Dijkstra alone cannot handle negatives - by a clever composition: add a virtual source, run BELLMAN-FORD (dart 046) once to get a potential h(v) that REWEIGHTS every edge to w + h(u) - h(v) (now non-negative, shortest paths preserved), then run DIJKSTRA (dart 055) from each vertex and undo the shift, for O(V^2 log V + VE). Two credit corrections: this is Donald Bruce Johnson (1977, founding chair of Dartmouth CS), NOT David S. Johnson of 'Garey & Johnson' NP-completeness fame; and the reweighting/node-potential trick is not Johnson's invention - node potentials come from min-cost-flow theory (the Edmonds-Karp era) - his contribution is using them for all-pairs shortest paths. On sparse graphs it beats Floyd-Warshall (dart 096), O(VE log V) vs O(V^3). In real I-13 it is nothing new: it literally composes Bellman-Ford (046, the potential + negative-cycle check, a 1-D array) and Dijkstra (055, from each vertex on the reweighted graph), with the reweight w + h(u) - h(v) pure f64 (verified A->C = -3 with a negative edge in the mix); the distance output is a 2-D matrix (PS-004) - a textbook case of two landed features compounding with no new primitive, like Pollard p-1 (083).
spheres.kicker: dart 114 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE MOBIUS FUNCTION
spheres.credit: The eponym is real but the priority is not: Mobius introduced the function in an 1832 paper on INVERTING SERIES (analysis, not number theory). The VALUES are Euler's, 1748: in the Introductio he wrote the reciprocal of the zeta series, product over p of (1 - p^-s) = sum mu(n)/n^s, whose coefficients are exactly the Mobius values. And Gauss beat Mobius by 31 years - Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), art. 81, gives 'sum of primitive roots mod p is congruent to mu(p-1)' - and Mobius was literally Gauss's astronomy student
spheres.source: A. Mobius 1832 (series inversion); L. Euler, Introductio 1748 (reciprocal zeta series); C. F. Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 81, 1801
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - factor n by trial division: if any prime appears squared, mu(n) = 0; otherwise mu(n) = (-1)^k for k distinct primes (verified mu(1)=1, mu(30)=-1, mu(12)=0). The INVERSION phi(n) = sum over d|n of mu(d)*(n/d) is a divisor loop of integer multiply/add (verified phi(12) = 4, recovering Euler's totient from n). All exact f64 integers. It ties the sieve (dart 017) and Euler's totient (dart 108); mu is the corpus's cleanest three-valued object (+1 / 0 / -1), and inversion is the number-theory analogue of undoing a running sum.
spheres.blurb: The Mobius function mu(n) is a three-valued fingerprint: 0 if a square divides n, else (-1)^k by whether n has an even or odd number of distinct primes. Tiny, but it powers MOBIUS INVERSION - recovering a function f from its divisor-sums g(n)=sum over d|n of f(d), via f(n)=sum over d|n of mu(d)g(n/d) - the backbone of sieves, inclusion-exclusion, and multiplicative number theory. The eponym is real but the priority is not: Mobius's 1832 paper was about INVERTING SERIES (an analysis result), while the function's VALUES are Euler's from 1748 (in the Introductio, the reciprocal of the zeta series product over p of (1-p^-s) = sum mu(n)/n^s has exactly these coefficients), and Gauss beat Mobius by 31 years (Disquisitiones 1801, art. 81, sum of primitive roots mod p congruent to mu(p-1)) - and Mobius was literally Gauss's astronomy student. In real I-13 it is nothing new: factor n by trial division, flag a square (mu = 0), else count distinct primes for the sign (verified mu(1)=1, mu(30)=-1, mu(12)=0), and the inversion phi(n) = sum over d|n of mu(d)(n/d) is a divisor loop of integer multiply/add (verified phi(12) = 4, recovering the totient) - tying the sieve (017) and Euler's totient (108), the cleanest three-valued object in the corpus.
spheres.kicker: dart 115 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE RABIN CRYPTOSYSTEM
spheres.credit: The eponym is correct - Michael O. Rabin invented the squaring trapdoor - but the object usually called 'the Rabin cryptosystem' (bare encryption c = m^2 mod n) is the textbook simplification. Year trap: the standard citation is 1979 (MIT/LCS/TR-212, January 1979), but the trapdoor first appeared in 1978 in 'Digitalized Signatures' (Foundations of Secure Computation). The MIT-official title uses 'Digitalized' (frequently mis-cited as 'Digitized'). It is the first scheme provably as hard to break as FACTORING (RSA-050 only conjectures this), via a reduction - which also makes it vulnerable to a chosen-ciphertext attack (a decryption oracle lets gcd factor n)
spheres.source: M. O. Rabin, MIT/LCS/TR-212, 1979; 'Digitalized Signatures and Public Key Functions as Intractable as Factorization', Foundations of Secure Computation, 1978; CRT (dart 047); RSA (dart 050)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - encryption c = m^2 mod n is one step of the bignum modexp engine (darts 032/035/050, exponent 2); decryption is two modexps (the p = 3 mod 4 root shortcut r = c^((p+1)/4) mod p on each prime) plus a CRT recombine (dart 047), exactly the RSA machinery (dart 050) reused. The FOUR candidate roots come out cleanly (verified {13, 20, 57, 64} for n=77, all squaring to 15 mod 77; the true m=20 is one of them, so the receiver needs redundancy to pick it). A real modulus wants a 2048-bit prime - bignum (dart 050's addition), which the corpus has; the toy case runs in f64.
spheres.blurb: The Rabin cryptosystem encrypts by SQUARING mod n = pq: c = m^2 mod n. Decrypting means a square root mod n, which needs the factors p and q - and its beauty is a PROOF that recovering the plaintext is provably AS HARD AS FACTORING n, a guarantee RSA (dart 050) only conjectures. Its quirk: mod a product of two primes every ciphertext has FOUR square roots, so the receiver must add redundancy (a header, a hash) to know which is the message. The eponym is correct - Michael Rabin invented the squaring trapdoor - with two footnotes: the trapdoor first appeared in a 1978 paper ('Digitalized Signatures', in Foundations of Secure Computation), the full cryptosystem in the 1979 MIT report (whose longer title is 'Digitalized Signatures and Public Key Functions as Intractable as Factorization'; spelled 'Digitalized', not 'Digitized'); and the same reduction proof that gives its security also makes it vulnerable to a chosen-ciphertext attack (a decryption oracle returning a different root lets gcd factor n - the proof cuts both ways). In real I-13 it is nothing new: encryption c = m^2 mod n is one bignum modexp step (exponent 2, darts 032/035/050), decryption is two modexps (the p = 3 mod 4 root shortcut) plus a CRT recombine (dart 047), all the RSA machinery reused - the four roots come out cleanly (verified {13,20,57,64} for n=77, each squaring to 15). A real modulus wants a 2048-bit prime, i.e. bignum, which the corpus has.
spheres.kicker: dart 116 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: GOLOMB CODING
spheres.credit: The eponym is RIGHT (verified both directions): Solomon W. Golomb really did invent Golomb codes, in 'Run-length encodings' (IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory IT-12(3):399-401, 1966) - NOT a naming accident. But two corrections: Golomb did NOT prove optimality for geometric distributions - the proof that a Golomb code minimizes expected length among all prefix codes for a geometric source is Gallager & van Voorhis (1975); and Rice coding is the special case M = power-of-two (Rice & Plaunt 1971), a subset not a separate invention of the general concept
spheres.source: S. W. Golomb, 'Run-length encodings', IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory IT-12(3):399-401, 1966; Gallager & van Voorhis 1975 (optimality proof); Rice & Plaunt 1971 (M = 2^k special case)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - encode is q = n / M and r = n % M (integer div/mod, dart 001), then emit q one-bits + a zero (a loop writing bits) and the truncated-binary remainder via a compare-and-branch (if r < u write b bits else write r+u in b+1 bits) - bitwise (dart 029); decode is the mirror (count one-bits to a zero for q, read b remainder bits, conditionally read one more, reassemble n = q*M + r). Verified code lengths 3,4,4,5 for M=5 (values 0,3,7,12) with an exact round-trip. Rice (M = 2^k) needs no division at all - pure shifts. It ties Huffman (dart 006) as the entropy family: Huffman is optimal for arbitrary alphabets, Golomb the closed-form optimum for geometric ones, with no tree stored.
spheres.blurb: For data where small values dominate - run lengths, gaps, quiet audio samples - Golomb coding is the optimal prefix code: split each number n by a parameter M into a QUOTIENT floor(n/M) written in unary (q ones then a zero) and a REMAINDER n mod M written in truncated binary (most remainders in floor(log2 M) bits, a few in one more). It is the entropy stage of FLAC, JPEG-LS (LOCO-I), and Rice-coded deep-space telemetry, beating Huffman on skewed data. The eponym is genuinely correct (verified both directions): Solomon Golomb invented Golomb codes in 'Run-length encodings' (1966), not a naming accident - but two corrections: Golomb did NOT prove their optimality for a geometric source (that proof is Gallager and van Voorhis, 1975), and Rice coding is just the special case M = 2^k (Rice and Plaunt, 1971), a subset rather than a separate invention. In real I-13 it is nothing new: encode is q = n/M and r = n mod M (integer div/mod, dart 001), then q one-bits + a zero and the truncated-binary remainder via a compare-and-branch (bitwise, dart 029); decode is the mirror (verified code lengths 3,4,4,5 for M=5 on values 0,3,7,12, exact round-trip). Rice (M = 2^k) needs no division at all, and it ties Huffman (006) as the entropy family - Huffman optimal for arbitrary alphabets, Golomb the closed-form optimum for geometric ones, no tree stored.
spheres.kicker: dart 117 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: ADABOOST
spheres.credit: Freund & Schapire are the right eponyms for AdaBoost (EuroCOLT '95, LNCS 904; the Godel-winning journal version is JCSS 55:119-139, 1997 - so the algorithm is two years older than its usual 1997 date), but AdaBoost is NOT the first boosting algorithm and did not invent boosting. The FIRST booster is Schapire's 'The Strength of Weak Learnability' (1990, a recursive majority-of-three); Freund's boost-by-majority (1990/95) followed. The CONCEPT and the word 'boosting' are Kearns & Valiant (Kearns' unpublished Dec-1988 note 'Thoughts on Hypothesis Boosting'; Kearns & Valiant 1989 left the weak-vs-strong equivalence open). What is genuinely new in AdaBoost is the ADAPTIVITY - alpha_t set from the observed error each round, needing no advance lower bound gamma on the weak learner's edge. The now-standard alpha = 0.5*ln((1-e)/e), H = sign(sum alpha*h), D update exp(-alpha*y*h) is the {-1,+1} form of Schapire & Singer (1999); the original 1997 paper used {0,1} labels and beta = e/(1-e)
spheres.source: Freund & Schapire, EuroCOLT '95 (LNCS 904) / JCSS 55:119-139, 1997; Schapire, Machine Learning 5:197-227, 1990 (first booster); Kearns 1988 (unpublished) & Kearns-Valiant 1989 (the word/question); Schapire & Singer, Machine Learning 37:297-336, 1999 (the 0.5 ln form); Long & Servedio 2008/2010 (noise limit)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - example weights are an f64 array; each round is a weighted-error sum, one vote alpha = 0.5*ln((1-e)/e) computed with the corpus's ln series (the inverse of dart 106's exp), and a reweight D_i <- D_i * exp(-alpha*y*h); the final classifier is sign(sum alpha_t h_t). Verified on the +,-,+ 1-D parity that no single stump can split: weighted errors 1/3, 1/4, 1/6 give alphas 0.3466, 0.5493, 0.8047 (0.5 ln 2/3/5), and the three margins come out +0.6020, -0.0912, +1.0074 - signs +,-,+, all three correct. The samples-by-features design matrix a real weak learner scans is a 2-D array (PS-004); the 1-D stump sidesteps it. Pairs with random forest (dart 125): AdaBoost reweights sequentially (boosting, bias reduction), random forest resamples in parallel (bagging, variance reduction).
spheres.blurb: AdaBoost turns a pile of barely-better-than-random classifiers into one strong classifier. Keep a weight on every training example (start uniform); each round, train a weak learner (classically a one-split decision 'stump') to minimize the WEIGHTED error e, give it a vote alpha = 0.5*ln((1-e)/e), then MULTIPLY up the weights of the examples it got wrong (and down the ones it got right) so the next round is forced onto the still-failing examples; the final classifier is sign(sum alpha_t h_t). The point of 'Ada'/adaptive: alpha is computed FROM the observed error each round, so - unlike the boosters before it - you never need to know the weak learner's edge over random in advance. Credit corrections: AdaBoost is NOT the first booster (that is Schapire 1990, a recursive majority construction; Freund's boost-by-majority followed), and it did not coin 'boosting' - that concept and word are Kearns & Valiant (1988-89). Its genuine novelty is the adaptivity; the famous alpha = 0.5 ln((1-e)/e) form is later still (Schapire & Singer 1999, the original 1997 paper used {0,1} labels). It won the 2003 Godel Prize, and Long & Servedio (2008/2010) proved any convex-potential booster - AdaBoost included - can be driven below 50% by any nonzero label-noise rate. In real I-13 it is nothing new: weights in an f64 array, one ln per round (the corpus's series), verified on a +,-,+ parity one stump cannot do - errors 1/3, 1/4, 1/6, alphas 0.3466/0.5493/0.8047, margins +0.6020/-0.0912/+1.0074 (all correct). The real samples-by-features design matrix is a 2-D array (PS-004); it pairs with random forest (125) as the boosting/bagging twins.
spheres.kicker: dart 118 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: SHIFT-OR / BITAP
spheres.credit: Named 'Shift-Or' by Baeza-Yates & Gonnet (Baeza-Yates's Waterloo PhD thesis, ~1989; CACM 35(10):74-82, Oct 1992), but the bit-parallel shift-and-mask automaton was published ~25 years earlier by Balint Domolki (1964, Computational Linguistics 3:29-46, Hungarian Academy of Sciences) - though for SYNTACTIC ANALYSIS (a nondeterministic parser recognizer), not string search, so calling Domolki's paper 'the bitap algorithm' would be a retro-attribution; Baeza-Yates & Gonnet genuinely re-derived it for text search. Two more corrections: the original is Shift-OR (0 = match, counter-intuitive, saves one op per char), NOT the more intuitive Shift-AND; and full fuzzy INSERTION/DELETION (edit-distance) matching is Wu & Manber (1991/92, the agrep tool), not Baeza-Yates & Gonnet, who handled only mismatches/wildcards/classes. The nickname 'bitap' appears in NEITHER original paper (a later gloss for 'bit-parallel approximate'); any confident etymology should be hedged
spheres.source: Baeza-Yates & Gonnet, CACM 35(10):74-82, 1992 (and Baeza-Yates PhD, Waterloo); Balint Domolki 1964 (Computational Linguistics 3:29-46, the bit-vector automaton); Wu & Manber 1991/92 (agrep, indel/fuzzy)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the per-character masks are an f64 array indexed by code point (bit j = 0 where the pattern has that char at position j); the whole automaton state is one integer; each step is R = (R << 1) | mask[c] masked to m bits (bitwise, dart 029), and the match test is R & (1 << (m-1)) == 0. Verified for pattern 'abc' (masks a=110, b=101, c=011): reading a,a,b,c the state walks 7 -> 6 -> 6 -> 5 -> 3, the high bit clears, MATCH ending at index 3 (start 1). Its only table is the small per-character mask (alphabet-sized, not pattern-sized); the automaton STATE is one machine word, so the O(1)-working-space property survives directly on bounded arrays. It joins the string family (Boyer-Moore 061, KMP 063), but where those precompute size-m PATTERN tables, Shift-Or is the one that carries the whole matcher state in one integer.
spheres.blurb: Shift-Or (a.k.a. bitap) carries a whole string-search automaton inside a single machine word. Precompute a bitmask per character (bit j is 0 exactly where the pattern has that character at position j); state R starts all-ones; then per text character c, R = (R << 1) | mask[c], keeping m bits. A run of matched characters walks a 0 up through R, and when bit m-1 reaches 0 the whole pattern has matched - no table the size of the text, no backtracking, and it extends to FUZZY matching by carrying a few extra words. Credit corrections: Baeza-Yates & Gonnet named Shift-Or (1989/92), but the bit-parallel shift-and-mask automaton is Balint Domolki (1964), ~25 years earlier - though Domolki built a parser recognizer, not string search, so over-crediting him with 'the bitap algorithm' is itself an error; the reinvention for text is genuine. Also: the original is Shift-OR (0 = match), not Shift-AND; true insertion/deletion fuzzy matching is Wu & Manber (agrep, 1991/92), not Baeza-Yates & Gonnet; and the nickname 'bitap' is in neither original paper. In real I-13 it is nothing new: masks in an f64 array, the state in one integer, each step (R<<1)|mask masked to m bits (bitwise, dart 029), match when the high bit clears - verified pattern 'abc' with masks 110/101/011, R walking 7->6->6->5->3 to a match at index 1 (start), its only table the small per-character mask (alphabet-sized, not pattern-sized) and the automaton state one machine word, so O(1) working space holds directly.
spheres.kicker: dart 119 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE SCHNORR SIGNATURE
spheres.credit: The eponym is CORRECT (verify-both-directions): Claus-Peter Schnorr (Goethe University Frankfurt) really invented it, at CRYPTO '89 (LNCS 435:239-252, proceedings 1990) - NOT a naming accident. Date bust: it debuted at CRYPTO '89, not 1991 (the common '1991' cites the later Journal of Cryptology 4(3):161-174 version). But Schnorr did not invent discrete-log signatures (that is Taher Elgamal, 1985, whom his own paper cites) and the interactive-to-non-interactive transform is Fiat & Shamir (CRYPTO '86, pub. 1987) - the Schnorr SIGNATURE is Fiat-Shamir applied to Schnorr IDENTIFICATION; his genuine contribution is the COMPRESSION (a small prime-order-q subgroup, hashing the commitment WITH the message). Provable security is NOT Schnorr's: the first unforgeability proof (ROM, discrete-log) is Pointcheval & Stern's Forking Lemma (EUROCRYPT '96), and it is a LOOSE reduction. Patent bust: US 4,995,082 expired Feb 23, 2010 (20-years-from-filing under URAA), NOT 2008 (the pre-1995 17-from-grant rule) - so the tidy 'expired the year Bitcoin launched' story is false; Bitcoin used mature patent-free ECDSA in 2009, and Schnorr reached Bitcoin only with Taproot (BIP-340, 2021)
spheres.source: Schnorr, CRYPTO '89 (LNCS 435:239-252) / J. Cryptology 4(3):161-174, 1991; Elgamal 1985; Fiat & Shamir, CRYPTO '86 (pub. 1987); Pointcheval & Stern, EUROCRYPT '96 (Forking Lemma); US Patent 4,995,082 (exp. Feb 23, 2010); Bitcoin BIP-340 (2021)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - y = g^x, the commitment r = g^k, and the verification g^s * y^e are the bignum modular exponentiation the corpus already runs (darts 032/035/050); s = k - x*e mod q is one modular subtract. Verified with p=23, q=11, g=2, x=3, k=5, e=4: y=8, r=9, s=4, and g^s*y^e mod p = 2^4 * 8^4 = 9 == r, so the signature ACCEPTs. Only the challenge hash H(r,m) is stubbed (a real one is SHA, a bitwise/rotate build). It ties RSA (050) and Rabin (116) on primitives, and carries a live footgun the corpus can demonstrate: s is LINEAR in the nonce k, so signing two messages with the same k solves two linear equations for the private x - the same nonce-reuse flaw (shared with ECDSA) behind the 2010 PlayStation-3 and Bitcoin-wallet key extractions.
spheres.blurb: A Schnorr signature is a compact discrete-log signature: pick a random nonce k, commit r = g^k, hash the commitment WITH the message to a challenge e = H(r, m), and answer s = k - x*e mod q; the signature is (r, s), verified by checking g^s * y^e = r (because g^(k-xe) (g^x)^e = g^k). Short, fast, and provably unforgeable in the random-oracle model - now the signature under Bitcoin's Taproot. It composes three people's ideas: Elgamal's discrete-log problem, Fiat-Shamir's interactive-to-non-interactive trick, and Schnorr's compression. Credit: the eponym is CORRECT (Claus-Peter Schnorr, CRYPTO '89 - not the often-cited 1991), but discrete-log signatures are Elgamal's (1985), the non-interactive transform is Fiat & Shamir's (1986), and the security proof is Pointcheval & Stern's Forking Lemma (1996, a loose reduction). Schnorr's genuine contribution is the compression: a small prime-order-q subgroup and hashing the commitment with the message. And the patent (US 4,995,082) actually expired Feb 2010, NOT 2008 - so the story that it 'lapsed the year Bitcoin launched' is false on both ends; Satoshi used patent-free ECDSA in 2009 and Schnorr reached Bitcoin only with Taproot (2021). In real I-13 it is nothing new: y=g^x, r=g^k, and the verify g^s y^e are the corpus's modexp (032/035/050), s = k-xe mod q one modular subtract - verified p=23,q=11,g=2,x=3,k=5,e=4 giving y=8, r=9, s=4, g^s y^e = 9 = r, ACCEPT (only the hash is stubbed). It ties RSA (050) and Rabin (116), and shows the k-reuse footgun: s is linear in k, so two signatures under one nonce leak the private key.

spheres.title: BRENT'S METHOD
spheres.credit: The eponym OVER-credits Brent. The bracket-keeping secant+bisection hybrid ('zeroin', with guaranteed convergence) is Dekker's (1969, 'Finding a zero by means of successive linear interpolation'); Brent (1971) built directly on it and even lists 'Dekker's algorithm' as a keyword in his own paper. Brent's genuine additions are (1) inverse quadratic interpolation and (2) the safety inequalities that decide when to fall back to bisection - i.e. the safeguarded combination with a proven bound, not any single step (IQI, the secant method, and regula falsi all long predate him). Year bust: the algorithm is routinely dated '1973' (the Prentice-Hall book Algorithms for Minimization without Derivatives) but was published two years earlier in The Computer Journal 14(4):422-425, 1971 (received Aug 1970). The 'van Wijngaarden' in 'van Wijngaarden-Dekker-Brent' is essentially INSTITUTIONAL credit - Aad van Wijngaarden directed the Amsterdam Mathematisch Centrum where Dekker worked; there is no separate van Wijngaarden publication of this root-finder (and MathWorld even mis-spells it 'Deker'). 'Guaranteed convergence' is real but conditional: it needs a sign-changing bracket, so it cannot find even-multiplicity roots (a tangent touch)
spheres.source: R. P. Brent, Computer Journal 14(4):422-425, 1971 (not the 1973 book); T. J. Dekker 1969 (zeroin, the bracketed secant+bisection); Bus & Dekker 1975 (better worst-case bound); regula falsi (Rhind Papyrus, antiquity)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the whole method is a handful of f64 scalars: the secant update b - f(b)*(b-a)/(f(b)-f(a)), the bisection midpoint (a+b)/2, the sign test f(a)*f(s) < 0, and |.| comparisons for the safeguards - no array at all. Verified on f(x) = x^2 - 2 from bracket [1,2]: the secant core converges to 1.4142135623730951 (the nearest f64 to sqrt 2), with root^2 = 2.0000000000000004; the fuller Brent hybrid visibly fires bisection, secant, and inverse quadratic interpolation while the bracket only shrinks. The float division (dart 001) carries it. It composes the corpus's root-finders (bisection, secant, Newton) into one SAFEGUARDED solver; the honest gap is that i13 runs the secant core, while true Brent's bracket bookkeeping and the IQI branch are a real (small) build on top.
spheres.blurb: Brent's method is the default scalar root-finder in SciPy's brentq and the engine under MATLAB's fzero. Keep a bracket [a,b] that always straddles the root; each step, TRY a fast method (inverse quadratic interpolation or the secant step) but FALL BACK to bisection whenever the fast step would leave the bracket or stall - so you get secant-like speed with bisection's guarantee, and convergence is never lost. Credit corrections: the bracket-keeping secant+bisection 'zeroin' is Dekker's (1969), which Brent (1971) built on and keyworded as 'Dekker's algorithm'; Brent's genuine additions are inverse quadratic interpolation and the safety inequalities for falling back to bisection - the safeguarded combination with a proven bound, not any single step. It is routinely mis-dated '1973' (the Prentice-Hall book) but debuted in The Computer Journal 14(4):422-425, 1971; the 'van Wijngaarden' name is institutional (he directed the Amsterdam centre where Dekker worked - no separate publication). 'Guaranteed convergence' is real but conditional: it needs a sign-changing bracket, so it misses even-multiplicity roots. In real I-13 it is nothing new: the entire state is a few f64 scalars (secant update, midpoint, sign test, |.| safeguards) - no array - verified on x^2 - 2 from [1,2], the secant core reaching 1.4142135623730951 (nearest f64 to sqrt 2, root^2 = 2.0000000000000004), the full hybrid firing bisection/secant/IQI while the bracket only shrinks; the honest gap is that i13 runs the secant core while true Brent's bracket bookkeeping and IQI branch are a small build on top.

spheres.title: THE QUADRATIC SIEVE
spheres.credit: The eponym is Carl Pomerance (invented the quadratic sieve at the University of Georgia, 1981), but the congruence-of-squares HEART - looking for x^2 = y^2 (mod n) rather than Fermat's exact x^2 - y^2 = n - is Maurice Kraitchik's (1920s) and is, by Pomerance's own account, the basis of most modern factoring. QS's direct parent is Richard Schroeppel's LINEAR SIEVE (c. 1976-77), which Schroeppel never formally published. Two more corrections: 'fastest factoring algorithm ever' is wrong - QS was champion for large hard numbers only from the early/mid 1980s until the number field sieve overtook it (~1990-96, above ~100-120 digits); it remains the simplest/fastest below ~100 digits. And QS's runtime is HEURISTIC/conjectural - Dixon's method (1981) is the sibling with a RIGOROUS proven subexponential bound (via random x), which QS trades away for practical speed. The record-setting variant is MPQS (multiple-polynomial), credit contested between Davis & Holdridge (Sandia) and Montgomery; RSA-129 (1994) fell to double-large-prime MPQS across ~600 volunteers, not plain QS and not Pomerance
spheres.source: Carl Pomerance 1981 (conception; analysis pub. 1982, EUROCRYPT '84); Kraitchik 1920s (congruence of squares); Schroeppel c.1976-77 (linear sieve, unpublished); Dixon 1981 (rigorous random-squares); Fermat c.1643; general NFS (Buhler-Lenstra-Pomerance 1993)
spheres.i13_recommend: the congruence-of-squares CORE is LIT end to end. The sieve interval Q(a) = a^2 - n near sqrt(n) is an f64 array; trial-dividing each Q by a small factor base to test smoothness is integer mod; combining two smooth relations whose exponent parities match gives x^2 = y^2 (mod n) via a bignum multiply; and the split is Euclid's gcd (dart 027). Verified for n=1649: a=41 gives Q=32=2^5 and a=43 gives Q=200=2^3*5^2 (matching parity), so x = 41*43 = 114, y = sqrt(32*200) = 80, and 114^2 = 80^2 = 1453 (mod 1649), with gcd(114-80,1649) = 17 and gcd(114+80,1649) = 97 - factoring 1649 = 17 x 97. The FRONTIER this toy skips is the general relation-selection step: choosing which relations combine is Gaussian elimination over GF(2) on the exponent-parity vectors, a genuine 2-D bit matrix (PS-004). Two hand-picked relations dodge it; the real sieve cannot.
spheres.blurb: The quadratic sieve factors n without ever guessing a factor. SIEVE the values Q(a) = a^2 - n near sqrt(n) for ones that are SMOOTH (factor completely over a small prime base); combine two smooth relations whose combined prime exponents are all even, so their product is a PERFECT SQUARE, giving a congruence of squares x^2 = y^2 (mod n); then gcd(x - y, n) splits n at least half the time (the sieve gathers spare relations, so it almost always succeeds). It was the fastest classical method for large hard numbers in its era and remains the simplest below ~100 digits. Credit: the eponym is Pomerance (1981), but the congruence-of-squares heart is Kraitchik's (1920s), and QS's direct parent is Schroeppel's unpublished linear sieve (c. 1976-77). Corrections: it was NOT the 'fastest ever' - the number field sieve overtook it (~1990-96, above ~100-120 digits); and its runtime is heuristic, unlike Dixon's rigorously-proven random-squares cousin (1981), whose proof QS trades for speed. RSA-129 (1994) fell to the multiple-polynomial variant (MPQS) run by ~600 volunteers, not plain QS. In real I-13 the congruence-of-squares core is LIT: the sieve interval is an f64 array, smoothness is integer mod, the combine is a bignum multiply, and the split is Euclid's gcd (dart 027) - verified n=1649, a=41 -> Q=32=2^5, a=43 -> Q=200=2^3*5^2, combining to 114^2 = 80^2 = 1453 (mod 1649), gcd -> 17 and 97. The frontier it skips is relation selection: Gaussian elimination over GF(2) on the exponent-parity vectors, a genuine 2-D bit matrix (PS-004) the real sieve cannot avoid.

spheres.title: SEPARATING AXIS THEOREM
spheres.credit: 'Separating Axis Theorem' is a computer-graphics/game-development LABEL, not a classical mathematics theorem name - mathematicians call the underlying result the hyperplane separation theorem (Minkowski's separation theorem). Minkowski (Geometrie der Zahlen, 1896) proves only that a separating hyperplane EXISTS for disjoint convex sets; he does NOT show that testing a finite list of directions suffices - the load-bearing algorithmic content is the finite candidate-axis reduction for polytopes (face normals + edge cross-products), and the 'invented vs made efficient' credit is Baraff (1990, general polytope) and Gottschalk-Lin-Manocha (1996, the 15-axis OBB test), popularized by Chris Hecker's mid-1990s game-physics columns. Two hard corrections: in 3-D the edge normals ALONE are insufficient - you must also test the 9 edge-edge cross-products, or two boxes yield a false 'collision'; and SAT is valid for CONVEX shapes only (concave shapes must be decomposed first). The 'axis' is the line ORTHOGONAL to the separating plane (the projection direction), not the plane itself; and unit-normalizing each axis with a sqrt is a myth-cost - scaling an axis scales both projected intervals equally, so the raw edge-normal needs only +, -, *
spheres.source: Minkowski, Geometrie der Zahlen, 1896 (existence); Baraff, SIGGRAPH 1990 (polytope separating plane); Gottschalk, Lin & Manocha, SIGGRAPH '96 (OBBTree, 15-axis test); Chris Hecker, Game Developer 1996-97; Brunn 1887 / Klee & Rockafellar (terminology)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - hold each polygon as two parallel f64 arrays xs[] and ys[] (the PS-004 sidestep: no struct-of-pairs and no 2-D array; parallel scalar arrays carry the (x,y) vertices). For each edge the candidate axis is the perpendicular (-dy, dx) - pure subtraction; projecting a vertex is a dot product; the overlap test is min/max comparisons. Verified for triangles A={(0,0),(4,0),(0,3)} and B={(5,0),(9,0),(9,3)}: on axis (1,0) the projections are A=[0,4] and B=[5,9], maxA=4 < minB=5, gap = 1, so separated=1 (DISJOINT) - only one of the candidate axes had to be tested. And the usual sqrt normalization is unnecessary (scaling an axis scales both intervals equally), so raw +, -, * suffice. The honest scope limit is dimensional: the 2-D edge-normal test lands cleanly, but 3-D needs the 9 edge-edge cross-product axes too, which the corpus can compute but this dart does not.
spheres.blurb: The separating axis theorem: two convex shapes miss each other IF AND ONLY IF there is some direction along which their projected shadows do not overlap. For polygons you need only test a FINITE set of directions - the edge normals - and the moment one shows a gap you stop: they cannot be colliding. It is the collision test in countless 2-D game engines, and it is Minkowski's 1896 hyperplane-separation theorem in game-dev costume. Credit: 'Separating Axis Theorem' is a graphics label, not a classical math name (mathematicians say hyperplane separation theorem); Minkowski (1896) proves only that a separating hyperplane EXISTS - the algorithmic content, the finite candidate-axis reduction, is Baraff (1990) and Gottschalk-Lin-Manocha (1996, the 15-axis OBB test), popularized by Chris Hecker. Hard corrections: in 3-D edge normals alone are INSUFFICIENT - you must add the 9 edge-edge cross-products, or two boxes report a false collision; SAT is convex-only (decompose concave shapes first); the 'axis' is the line orthogonal to the separating plane; and unit-normalizing with a sqrt is a myth-cost. In real I-13 it is nothing new: hold each polygon as two parallel f64 arrays xs[], ys[] (the PS-004 sidestep - no 2-D array), each edge normal is (-dy, dx), projection is a dot product, overlap is min/max compares - verified triangles A={(0,0),(4,0),(0,3)} vs B={(5,0),(9,0),(9,3)}: on axis (1,0), A=[0,4], B=[5,9], maxA=4 < minB=5, gap 1, separated (one axis sufficed), with no sqrt needed. The honest limit is dimensional: 2-D lands, 3-D needs the 9 edge-edge cross-product axes too.

spheres.title: PERSISTENT SEGMENT TREE
spheres.credit: Path copying is NOT a Driscoll-Sarnak-Sleator-Tarjan (DSST) invention: in 'Making Data Structures Persistent' (STOC 1986; JCSS 38(1):86-124, 1989) the authors themselves credit path copying for fully persistent search trees to Myers (AVL Dags, 1982/84), Krijnen & Meertens (1983), Reps-Teitelbaum-Demers (1983), and Swart (1985) - four independent discoveries. The persistent segment tree deliberately uses that OLDER, simpler O(log n)-space path copying, NOT DSST's headline result (the fat-node / node-copying methods that cut space to O(1) amortized). 'Segment tree' is a genuine naming collision: Bentley's 1977 segment tree (from Klee's measure problem) stores intervals and answers stabbing queries, a DIFFERENT object from the competitive-programming 'segment tree', a balanced tree over ARRAY INDICES holding range aggregates. Sarnak & Tarjan's 1986 CACM paper, often cited as the origin, is an APPLICATION (planar point location) on a persistent SEARCH tree with limited node copying - not a persistent Bentley segment tree and not path copying. 'Persistent segment tree' is a competitive-programming folklore name (1990s-2000s), and path copying yields FULL persistence for free even though most uses exercise only a linear version chain
spheres.source: path copying: Myers 1982/84, Krijnen & Meertens 1983, Reps-Teitelbaum-Demers 1983, Swart 1985 (per DSST's own citations); DSST, STOC 1986 / JCSS 38(1):86-124, 1989 (the O(1)-space methods); Bentley 1977 (the classical/interval segment tree); Sarnak & Tarjan, CACM 29(7):669-679, 1986 (planar point location)
spheres.i13_recommend: the PRINCIPLE is already LIT. An i13 array update v[i] <- e yields a NEW array and leaves the old one aliased-free (functional/value-semantic update) - the exact immutability a persistent structure embodies. Verified: from A=[5,2,3,8], querying range-sum[1,3] gives 13; forking version 2 by setting A[2]=10 gives a v2 range-sum[1,3] of 20, while v1 is STILL queryable at 13 after v2 diverged - both versions coexist and disagree by exactly the delta (10-3=7). That value semantics is why the corpus can model versioning at all. The FRONTIER is the cost refinement: i13's array update conceptually copies the whole array (O(n) fresh cells), while a persistent segment tree copies only the O(log n) nodes on the changed root-to-leaf path (3 new nodes here, sharing 4), which needs shared POINTER nodes / an arena (PS-015). The corpus has the semantics for free; it lacks the sharing that makes it cheap.
spheres.blurb: A persistent segment tree keeps every past version queryable. A segment tree answers range-sums in O(log n); a PERSISTENT one, on each update, copies only the O(log n) nodes on the changed root-to-leaf path and SHARES everything else with the previous version - so two versions cost a path, not a whole tree, and version 1 answers exactly as it did before version 2 existed. It is the same immutability I-13's value-semantic arrays are built on. Credit: path copying is NOT DSST's invention - their own paper credits it to Myers (1982) and three others independently; DSST's real novelty is the fat-node / node-copying methods that cut space to O(1) amortized, which the persistent segment tree deliberately does NOT use (it uses the older, simpler O(log n) path copying). 'Segment tree' is a naming collision: Bentley's 1977 interval structure vs the competitive-programming array-aggregate tree; and Sarnak-Tarjan's 1986 paper, often cited as origin, is a different structure (persistent search tree for planar point location). In real I-13 the principle is already LIT: an array update v[i] <- e yields a NEW array leaving the old aliased-free - functional update, the same immutability - verified from A=[5,2,3,8], range-sum[1,3]=13, then A[2]=10 forks version 2 with range-sum[1,3]=20 while version 1 is STILL 13 (both coexist, differ by exactly 7). The frontier is cost: i13's update conceptually copies the whole array (O(n)), while the persistent tree copies only the O(log n) path (3 new nodes, sharing 4) - which needs shared pointer nodes / an arena (PS-015). The corpus has the semantics for free; it lacks the cheap sharing.

spheres.title: RANDOM FOREST
spheres.credit: The name is not the invention: Breiman's 2001 paper ('Random Forests', Machine Learning 45(1):5-32, with Adele Cutler) is the eponym and popularizer, but Tin Kam Ho coined 'random decision forests' and published the FIRST algorithm - the random subspace method - in 1995 (ICDAR, pp. 278-282; journal treatment IEEE PAMI 20(8):832-844, 1998). Two randomness mechanisms get merged: Ho's random subspace picks a random feature subset ONCE per tree, while Amit & Geman (1997) and Breiman's RF pick a random feature subset at EACH node/split - Breiman's specific contribution is bagging + per-node random feature selection on CART trees. Bagging is a separate, earlier Breiman result (1996; tech report 1994) and is NOT itself a random forest (no random feature selection). Adele Cutler is a genuine co-developer (co-holder of the 'Random Forests' registered trademark, filed 2005/reg. 2006, and co-author of the reference Fortran) routinely erased by the single-name story. RF is a BAGGING/variance-reduction method (majority vote of decorrelated trees), NOT boosting; and randomized-tree committees existed before 1995 (Heath, Kasif & Salzberg 1993), so Ho's precise 'first' is the first random-SUBSPACE forest
spheres.source: Tin Kam Ho, ICDAR 1995 (pp. 278-282) / IEEE PAMI 20(8):832-844, 1998 (random subspace, coined the term); Breiman, Machine Learning 45(1):5-32, 2001 (single-authored; Adele Cutler co-developed the method + reference Fortran); Breiman 1996/1994 (bagging); Amit & Geman 1997 (per-node random splits); Heath-Kasif-Salzberg 1993 (earlier tree committees)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - a tree's prediction is a threshold compare x <= t; per-class vote tallies are f64 arrays; the forest decision is argmax over the counts. The stdlib seeded PRNG supplies the bootstrap row indices and the random feature-subset draw, so the whole forest is reproducible under a seed. Verified on 5 samples (true A,A,A,B,B) with three stumps each splitting on one feature (rule value<=5 -> A else B): each stump scores 4/5 = 80% (each misses a DIFFERENT row), but the majority vote scores 5/5 = 100% - the ensemble strictly beats every member because their errors land on different rows and the vote outvotes each lone mistake. The real samples-by-features design matrix is a 2-D array (PS-004) - the same want AdaBoost (dart 118) hits; the two are the campaign's bagging/boosting pair, and both meet the matrix wall the moment they leave one feature.
spheres.blurb: A random forest grows many decision trees - each on a bootstrap RESAMPLE of the data and splitting on a RANDOM subset of features - then takes the majority vote. The randomness DECORRELATES the trees, so their independent errors cancel and the ensemble beats every single tree even when each tree is mediocre. It is BAGGING (parallel, variance-reducing), the opposite twin of AdaBoost's boosting (sequential, bias-reducing). Credit: Breiman's 2001 paper (single-authored) is the eponym and popularizer, but 'random decision forests' and the first algorithm - the random subspace method - are Tin Kam Ho's (1995). Two randomness mechanisms get merged: Ho picks a random feature subset once per tree; Amit & Geman (1997) and Breiman pick one at each node - Breiman's specific contribution is bagging + per-node random features on CART trees. Bagging is a separate, earlier Breiman result (1996) and is NOT itself a random forest; Cutler is a genuine co-developer (co-holder of the registered trademark) routinely erased; and RF is a bagging/variance-reduction method, not boosting. In real I-13 it is nothing new: a tree's prediction is a threshold compare x <= t, per-class vote tallies are f64 arrays, the forest decision is argmax, and the seeded PRNG supplies the bootstrap rows and feature subset (reproducible under a seed) - verified 5 samples (A,A,A,B,B), three stumps each 4/5 = 80% (each missing a different row), the majority vote 5/5 = 100%, strictly beating every member. The real samples-by-features design matrix is a 2-D array (PS-004) - the same want AdaBoost (118) hits; the two are the campaign's bagging/boosting pair.

spheres.blurb: On 2026-08-19 the I-13 compiler got its own conformance benchmark, and its whole design is a refusal to lie by rounding up. The frozen contract I13-BC-1.0 keeps apart four facts that benchmarks usually collapse: you built something (implementation progress), you checked it yourself (self-verification, independence L0), someone independent sealed holdouts and graded it (L1/L2), and an official external service produced a bundle (L3) - and it forbids the words 'official' or 'Terminal-Bench PASS' in any report without that bundle. The honest grade curve climbs v0.3 to v0.8 (public 53,57,61,64,68,72 of 96), each version earning exactly one new P0 semantic gate with no regression. This fold reads every bit of the drop and runs its two demonstrable hearts live: core.i13, the 8-channel routing core (0 PROCESS to 7 KERNEL) in the topology [ 0 | HTML(00) | 0 ] where I-13 owns the routing law and the host owns I/O - verified on the real compiler at CORE_OK=1, ROUTES=56 (8x7 ordered routes, no channel to itself), with the four I-13 planes exact and the 12-verbs-plus-1-declaration = 13 alphabet holding; and the refusal-detector probe, which reproduces a shipped tool's 32-marker keyword detector verbatim and is wrong 9 times out of 12 on a labeled set (5 false positives where a correct legal or clinical answer is scored a refusal on 'illegal' or 'harmful', 4 false negatives where a genuine refusal uses none of the 32 strings, 1 window-blind miss past the 100-token cap) - the existence of each failure class is LIT (one string is an existence proof), the 75% rate is AMBER (a small adversarial set). spheres.title: THE PRATT PARSER
spheres.credit: Vaughan Pratt, 'Top Down Operator Precedence', POPL 1973 (pp. 41-51) - the terms nud (null denotation), led (left denotation), and 'binding power' are his. NOT the 2000s revival: Douglas Crockford POPULARIZED it (Beautiful Code, 2007; JSLint), Bob Nystrom taught it (2011), matklad made it a default (2020) - none invented it. It IMPROVES on Floyd's operator-precedence grammars (1963) - Floyd is BOTTOM-UP and table-driven on precedence relations between token pairs; Pratt is TOP-DOWN with precedence carried on the tokens and no grammar - do not collapse the two. 'Precedence climbing' (Clarke 1986, independently and without citing Pratt; named by Norvell ~1999) is the binary-infix SPECIAL CASE, per Andy Chu 2016 - not a rival, not identical in full generality.
spheres.source: Pratt, POPL 1973; Floyd, JACM 10:316-333, 1963 (operator-precedence grammars); Dijkstra shunting-yard 1961 / Samelson-Bauer 1960 (iterative stack, same problem different shape); Clarke 1986 + Norvell ~1999 (precedence climbing); Andy Chu 2016 (the reconciliation)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - and it opens the PARSER family. A parser must return a value AND how far it got; I-13 functions return one value, but an array IS one value, so a function returns [value, pos] and threads the cursor with no mutable state (a real 2-element array return, verified working). Tokens are an f64 array with operators as sentinel tags (PLUS=-1 lbp 10, STAR=-2 lbp 20, END=-9); the recursive routine swallows operators while their binding power exceeds a threshold. Verified: parsing [1,+,2,*,3] gives value 7 via tree (+ 1 (* 2 3)) - STAR's 20 clears the '+' threshold 10 so 2*3 groups first; a precedence-blind left-fold would give 9. The same [value,pos] trick carries recursive descent (128) and packrat (129); it resonates with the 8/19 benchmark's P1-002 target, 'expression precedence and associativity'.
spheres.blurb: A Pratt parser gives every operator a binding power and lets one recursive routine parse the whole expression - no grammar and no precedence table between token pairs. Descending into the right operand of '+', it raises a minimum-binding-power threshold so a following '*' can still grab its operands but a following '+' cannot; that threshold IS precedence. Every token carries at most two tiny actions - a nud (null denotation) for when it starts an expression and a led (left denotation) for when it follows something - and the parser is top-down, table-free, and trivially extensible. Credit: it is Vaughan Pratt, POPL 1973 ('Top Down Operator Precedence'), not the 2000s revival - Crockford popularized it in Beautiful Code (2007) and JSLint, but nud/led/binding-power are Pratt's own. It improves on Floyd's bottom-up operator-precedence grammars (1963), it does not restate them; and 'precedence climbing' (Clarke 1986, named ~1999) is its binary-infix special case, not a rival (Andy Chu, 2016). Left recursion is the easy, natural case here, not a defect. In real I-13 it is nothing new and opens the parser family: a function returns [value, pos] (a real array return) to thread the cursor with no mutable state, tokens are an f64 array with operators as sentinel tags, and the recursive routine swallows operators while their binding power beats the threshold (verified [1,+,2,*,3] -> 7, tree (+ 1 (* 2 3)), where a precedence-blind fold gives 9).

spheres.title: THE EARLEY PARSER
spheres.credit: Jay Earley - PhD thesis (Carnegie-Mellon, 1968) and the widely-read CACM 13(2):94-102, 1970 - for the general context-free RECOGNIZER (predict/scan/complete over origin-tagged dotted items). Unlike CYK (dart 093) it needs NO Chomsky Normal Form and handles left recursion, ambiguity, and epsilon rules directly - conflating the two erases the whole point. But three parts are NOT Earley's: the original nullable/epsilon-rule bug in COMPLETE was first patched by Aho-Ullman (1972) and cleanly by Aycock-Horspool (2002); the CORRECT parse-forest is Elizabeth Scott (2008) - Earley's own 1970 tree sketch over-generates; and linear time on every LR-regular grammar (removing the right-recursion O(n^2) trap) is Joop Leo (1991). The dotted-item notation A -> alpha . beta is Knuth's LR(k) (1965); the 'chart parsing' framing is Martin Kay's (1980).
spheres.source: Earley, CACM 13(2):94-102, 1970 (thesis 1968); Knuth 1965 (dotted items); Aho-Ullman 1972 + Aycock-Horspool 2002 (nullable fix); Joop Leo 1991 (linear right recursion); Elizabeth Scott 2008 (correct SPPF forest); CYK / dart 093 (requires CNF)
spheres.i13_recommend: the RECOGNITION VERDICT for a fixed grammar runs today. The demo's grammar S -> a S b | epsilon (augmented gamma -> S) accepts exactly the balanced language a^n b^n; the input is an f64 code-point array (I-13 has no strings) and a matched-outer-pair recursion rec(lo,hi) recognizes it exactly (verified 'aabb' [97,97,98,98] -> ACCEPT, 'aab' -> REJECT, 'abb' -> REJECT). The FRONTIER is the general engine: Earley's chart is one item-set per gap between tokens, and a general item set is a 2-D array (PS-004) whose entries are dotted items carrying an origin (a record / node arena, PS-015). The demo animates the real S0..S4 chart with predict/scan/complete; the compiler grounds the accept/reject that a fixed-grammar recognizer proves.
spheres.blurb: Earley parsing recognizes ANY context-free grammar directly - rules written the natural way, no Chomsky Normal Form, and left recursion, ambiguity, and empty rules handled as-is. It keeps one state set per gap between input tokens; each Earley item is a rule with a dot marking progress plus the origin position where the match began, [A -> alpha . beta, j]. Three moves fill the sets left to right: PREDICT adds a rule's items when its symbol is expected, SCAN advances items across a matching token, COMPLETE advances the parent when a rule finishes; accept iff the completed start item lands in the final set. Credit: the recognizer is Jay Earley (thesis 1968, CACM 1970) and it is correct and general - but the nullable-rule bug was fixed by Aho-Ullman (1972) then Aycock-Horspool (2002), the correct parse-forest is Elizabeth Scott (2008, since Earley's 1970 tree sketch over-generates), and linear time on LR-regular grammars is Joop Leo (1991); it is O(n^2) on unambiguous grammars, not always O(n^3). Unlike CYK (093) it needs no CNF - that IS the point. In real I-13 the recognition verdict for a fixed grammar runs: S -> a S b | eps accepts exactly a^n b^n via a matched-pair recursion over an f64 code array (verified aabb ACCEPT, aab/abb REJECT); the frontier is the general chart, one item-set per gap = a 2-D array (PS-004) of dotted items (PS-015).

spheres.title: THE RECURSIVE DESCENT
spheres.credit: Described in 1961, independently and near-simultaneously, by Ned Irons ('A Syntax Directed Compiler for ALGOL 60', CACM 4(1):51-55, January - the first parser of any kind fully described in print, general/left-corner) and Peter Lucas (IBM Vienna, December - the top-down parser built from mutually recursive procedures, one per metalinguistic variable). Niklaus Wirth POPULARIZED it through Pascal and the PL/0 teaching compiler in the 1970s; he did not invent it. Do not erase either 1961 author for the other. The predictive form is exactly the LL(k) grammar class (Lewis-Stearns 1968; Knuth's 'Top-Down Syntax Analysis' 1971, FIRST/FOLLOW). Myth: it is obsolete - GCC (since 3.4) and Clang are hand-written recursive descent. Myth: it needs backtracking - the LL(1) predictive form never backtracks and is linear.
spheres.source: Irons, CACM 4(1):51-55, 1961; Lucas, Elektronische Rechenanlagen 3, 1961; Backus-Naur (BNF, ALGOL 60, 1959-60); Lewis-Stearns 1968 (LL(k)); Knuth, Acta Informatica 1(2), 1971; Wirth (Pascal/PL/0, 1970s); GCC 3.4+ and Clang (hand-written RD)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - and it is a door already open: I-13's OWN compiler is a hand-written recursive-descent parser (one function per grammar rule). The classic expr/term/factor grammar runs over an f64 code-point array, each rule a recursive function returning [value, pos] (the array-return thread); parentheses re-enter expr; precedence is the call hierarchy (factor below term below expr), needing no table. Verified: 2*(3+4) = 14 with endpos 7 (all input consumed), 2*3+4 = 10, (2+3)*4 = 20. The one guard I-13 forces is a bounds check before reading past the input, since out-of-range indexing is rejected. Pairs with Pratt (126): same answers, two paradigms - recursive descent puts precedence in the GRAMMAR SHAPE, Pratt puts it on the TOKENS.
spheres.blurb: Recursive descent is the most direct way to turn a grammar into a program: write one function per grammar rule, and each function calls the functions for the symbols on its right-hand side, so the tree of calls at run time IS the parse tree. For arithmetic you write expr() (handles + and -), term() (handles * and /), and factor() (numbers and parenthesized sub-expressions); precedence needs no table - it is the nonterminal hierarchy, and parentheses re-enter expr() at the bottom. Credit: it was described in 1961, independently, by Ned Irons (January, the first parser described in print) and Peter Lucas (December, mutually recursive procedures one per rule) - a decade before Pascal; Niklaus Wirth made it famous but did not invent it. The predictive LL(1) form (one-token lookahead) never backtracks and is linear-time - backtracking recursive descent is a slower, distinct variant. It is not obsolete: GCC (since 3.4) and Clang are hand-written recursive descent, chosen over generated LR tables for error messages and control. In real I-13 it is nothing new and a door already open - the compiler's own parser is one of these - with each rule a recursive function returning [value, pos], parentheses re-entering expr, and precedence as the call hierarchy (verified 2*(3+4)=14 endpos 7, 2*3+4=10, (2+3)*4=20).

spheres.title: THE PACKRAT PARSER
spheres.credit: Bryan Ford (MIT), 2002 - the MIT Master's thesis and the ICFP 2002 functional pearl coin 'packrat' and prove that memoizing every (rule, position) turns TDPL-style backtracking parsing into linear time. But PEG and packrat are TWO inventions: PEG (Parsing Expression Grammars, ordered choice, syntactic predicates, unambiguous by construction) is Ford's SEPARATE 2004 POPL paper; packrat is the 2002 linear-time execution. And neither the backtracking machinery nor memoization is Ford's: ordered-choice top-down backtracking is Birman's TS/gTS (Princeton dissertation 1970, advisor Ullman), formalized as TDPL/GTDPL by Aho-Ullman (1972); memoization is Donald Michie's ('memo functions', Nature 1968). Over-correction to avoid: 'always memoize, always faster' is false - full packrat is linear TIME at O(n) SPACE and is frequently SLOWER than plain backtracking, which is why LPeg (2008) and CPython's PEG parser (PEP 617, 2020) skip full packrat. Naive packrat also cannot handle left recursion (Warth-Douglass-Millstein 2008 seeding, or Hutchison's Pika 2020, are needed).
spheres.source: Ford, MIT thesis + ICFP 2002 (packrat); Ford, POPL 2004 (PEG); Birman 1970 / Aho-Ullman 1972 (TDPL/GTDPL backtracking); Michie, Nature 218, 1968 (memoization); LPeg (Medeiros-Ierusalimschy 2008, no memo); CPython PEP 617 (2020, selective memo)
spheres.i13_recommend: the ordered-choice PEG parse is LIT. Input is an f64 code array; each nonterminal (Add/Mul/Prim) is a recursive function returning [value, pos, ...], and ordered choice A <- e1 / e2 is sequential if-branches; verified 2*(3+4) -> value 14, endpos 7 (all consumed), 4 Prim parses (the bind-once form = the memoized equivalent). The distinctive packrat move - memoizing every (rule, position) - is a memo[rule][pos] table, i.e. a 2-D array (PS-004); I-13 expresses it by THREADING a memo array through the recursion, the same value-semantics-as-mutable-store pattern as the sieve. The live demo animates the real 11-cell / 5-hit table on 2*(3+4) (each cell computed once, five later requests are hits); the corpus has the mechanism (a threaded array), the frontier is making the memo table first-class.
spheres.blurb: A Parsing Expression Grammar (PEG) specifies syntax with ORDERED CHOICE: A <- e1 / e2 tries e1 first and falls back to e2 only on failure, so a PEG is unambiguous by construction rather than by after-the-fact disambiguation. The price is unlimited backtracking, which naive re-parsing pays by re-visiting the same position exponentially; a PACKRAT parser removes that cost by memoizing every (rule, position), so each is computed at most once - linear time, at linear space. Credit: packrat is Bryan Ford (MIT thesis + ICFP 2002), but PEG the grammar is his SEPARATE 2004 paper - two inventions often wrongly equated. Neither ingredient is his either: ordered-choice backtracking is Birman's TDPL (1970, formalized by Aho-Ullman 1972) and memoization is Donald Michie's (Nature, 1968). Do not claim 'always memoize, always faster': full packrat is linear time at O(n) SPACE and is often SLOWER than plain backtracking, which is why LPeg and CPython's PEG parser skip full memo; and naive packrat cannot handle left recursion without the Warth-Douglass-Millstein (2008) seeding trick. Ordered choice does not resolve ambiguity - it forbids it, always committing to the first match. In real I-13 the PEG parse is LIT (2*(3+4) -> 14, all 7 chars consumed via ordered-choice if-branches over an f64 code array); the memo table memo[rule][pos] is a 2-D array (PS-004) that I-13 threads as a value-semantic array (the sieve pattern), and the demo animates the real 11-cell / 5-hit table.

spheres.title: THE THOMPSON CONSTRUCTION
spheres.credit: Ken Thompson, 'Regular Expression Search Algorithm', CACM 11(6):419-422, June 1968 - compile a regex to an epsilon-NFA by structural recursion, then MATCH by keeping the set of all states at once and never backtracking (he generated IBM 7094 code at run time). But regex-to-automaton was on paper eight years earlier: McNaughton & Yamada (IRE Trans. EC-9, 1960) gave the first algorithmic regex<->state-graph, and Kleene (1956) proved the equivalence exists (with no build procedure) - the honest textbook name is the McNaughton-Yamada-Thompson construction. Thompson's NFA deliberately USES epsilon edges (compositional, linear-sized); the epsilon-FREE one-state-per-symbol construction is Glushkov's (1961). Myth: regex matching is inherently exponential / needs backtracking - Thompson showed O(mn) linear in 1968; the ReDoS blow-up is a property of the BACKTRACKING engines (Perl/PCRE) that abandoned his method. grep (1973) and ed are separate implementations; the DFA descendant is Aho's egrep (1979, a precomputed DFA; on-the-fly/lazy by the 1985 Eighth Edition).
spheres.source: Thompson, CACM 11(6):419-422, 1968; McNaughton-Yamada, IRE Trans. EC-9, 1960; Kleene 1956 (equivalence); Glushkov 1961 (epsilon-free position automaton); Aho egrep 1979 (precomputed DFA; on-the-fly/lazy by 1985); Russ Cox / RE2 2007 (revival); dart 119 shift-or (the same active-set bitmask)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the MATCHING half is a clean fit. Encode the input as an f64 array of code points (branch c==97 vs c==98, no strings needed) and hold the active NFA state-set as a single f64 integer bitmask (11 bits for (a|b)*abb, and up to 53 stay exact in f64), driven by I-13's bitwise ops. Each input symbol maps the mask to the next set (move + epsilon-closure, an OR of precomputed per-state closure masks); accept is one AND with the accepting bit. Verified for (a|b)*abb: 'aabb' [0,0,1,1] walks mask 151 -> 478 -> 478 -> 758 -> 1270, and 1270 & 1024 = 1024 -> ACCEPT; 'ab' halts at 758, bit 10 clear -> REJECT. It is Shift-Or's (dart 119) machinery on an NFA instead of a fixed pattern. BUILDING the NFA from an arbitrary regex wants a node structure (the string want + a node arena, PS-015); the transition/closure tables here are precomputed f64 arrays.
spheres.blurb: Thompson's construction compiles a regular expression into a nondeterministic finite automaton by structural recursion - each literal becomes two states on a labeled edge, and concatenation, alternation, and Kleene star glue sub-automata together with epsilon edges - giving about 2m states for a length-m regex. Its real insight is MATCHING without backtracking: keep the SET of every state the NFA could be in and advance them all in lockstep, which is O(mn) linear (and the reason grep is fast where backtracking engines suffer ReDoS blow-up). That active set is a bitmask - the same trick as Shift-Or (dart 119). Credit: the build-and-simulate is Thompson (CACM 1968), but McNaughton & Yamada put regex-to-automaton on paper in 1960 and Kleene proved the equivalence in 1956, so the honest name is the McNaughton-Yamada-Thompson construction; the epsilon-free sibling is Glushkov (1961). Regex matching is NOT inherently exponential - Thompson showed linear in 1968; the blow-up belongs to the backtracking engines that abandoned his method. In real I-13 it is nothing new: input as an f64 code array, the active set as one f64 bitmask, each move an OR of per-state epsilon-closure masks, accept one AND (verified (a|b)*abb: aabb -> 151,478,478,758,1270 ACCEPT; ab -> 758 REJECT). Building the NFA from an arbitrary regex wants a node arena (PS-015).

spheres.title: THE SUBSET CONSTRUCTION
spheres.credit: Michael O. Rabin & Dana S. Scott, 'Finite Automata and Their Decision Problems', IBM J. Res. Dev. 3(2):114-125, 1959 - they invent the NFA and prove NFA equivalent to DFA by the subset (powerset) construction, treating each DFA state as a SET of NFA states. Their 1976 Turing Award was for inventing NONDETERMINISM and the paper's decision-problem results, NOT the subset trick specifically - reducing their prize to 'the subset construction' undersells it. It is NOT Kleene's (Kleene 1956 equated regex with DETERMINISTIC automata, with no nondeterminism and no subset construction). Determinization is NOT minimization (that is Myhill-Nerode 1957/58 and Hopcroft's n log n, 1971 - a separate stage). And NFA->DFA (Rabin-Scott) is not regex->NFA (Thompson 1968 / McNaughton-Yamada 1960). The 2^n state count is a WORST-case upper bound, not typical - most NFAs determinize small, and RE2/Go/Rust build the DFA lazily at match time.
spheres.source: Rabin & Scott, IBM J. Res. Dev. 3(2):114-125, 1959; Turing Award 1976 (for nondeterminism); Kleene 1956; Myhill-Nerode 1957/58 + Hopcroft 1971 (minimization); Thompson 1968 (builds the NFA); RE2/Go/Rust (lazy DFA)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - a subset-state is one f64 bitmask (the reference VM computes AND/OR/XOR/shift by coercing operands as i64, so a subset can hold up to 63 NFA states with no extra structure), and the transition relation delta is a FLAT f64 array read at index state*2+sym. A DFA step is the OR of the live states' targets; a set accepts iff it contains the accept bit (one AND). Verified for (a|b)*a with delta=[3,1,0,0] and accept mask 2: 'abba' walks subset masks 1 -> 3 -> 1 -> 1 -> 3, final 3 & 2 = 2 -> ACCEPT; 'abb' -> 1 -> 3 -> 1 -> 1, final 1 & 2 = 0 -> REJECT; the DFA has exactly 2 reachable subsets of the 4 possible. It is the lazy / on-the-fly form, exactly what RE2 does. Pairs with Thompson (130): 130 BUILDS the NFA and simulates it, 131 DETERMINIZES it - the two halves of regex -> NFA -> DFA. A full delta for many states is a 2-D array (PS-004) flattened here to 1-D by hand.
spheres.blurb: A nondeterministic finite automaton can occupy many states at once, following every matching edge in parallel; the subset (powerset) construction makes it deterministic by treating the whole SET of possible NFA states as a single DFA state. Start from the start set (plus its epsilon-closure); to read a symbol, take the union of every current state's targets; a set is accepting if it contains an accept state. It proves nondeterminism buys no extra power - at a cost of up to 2^n states, though most NFAs stay small. Credit: it is Rabin & Scott (1959), who invented the NFA; their 1976 Turing Award was for NONDETERMINISM and the paper's decision problems, not the subset trick specifically. It is not Kleene's (he had only deterministic automata, 1956); determinization is not minimization (Myhill-Nerode 1957/58, Hopcroft 1971); and NFA->DFA is not regex->NFA (Thompson/McNaughton-Yamada). 2^n is a worst case, not the rule - RE2/Go/Rust build the DFA lazily at match time (a cached subset construction). In real I-13 it is nothing new: a subset-state is one f64 bitmask (up to 63 states, since the VM does bitwise as i64), delta is a flat f64 array at state*2+sym, a step is an OR of live targets, accept is one AND (verified (a|b)*a: abba -> masks 1,3,1,1,3 ACCEPT; abb -> 1,3,1,1 REJECT; 2 reachable subsets of 4). Pairs with Thompson (130) as the two halves of regex -> NFA -> DFA.
