spheres.title: THE MCCARTHY 91 FUNCTION
spheres.credit: John McCarthy devised it (~1968-70) as a deliberately hard-to-verify nested-recursion test case; '91' is its constant OUTPUT for n<=100, not a version or problem number. MIS-DATING to avoid: it does NOT originate in Manna's 1974 textbook (the most-cited source) - it was introduced in TWO 1970 papers, Manna & Pnueli (J.ACM 17(3):555-569) and Manna & McCarthy (Machine Intelligence 5), which give the first formal termination/validity proofs. Attribution: McCarthy devised it, Manna & Pnueli first proved it - do not credit the invention to Manna/Pnueli, but do not erase them either. It is structurally Ackermann-like (nested double recursion) but BOUNDED - it returns the constant 91, so the challenge is seeing it terminates and collapses, not taming explosive growth. It is total over ALL integers (returns 91 for every n<=100, including negatives), and is distinct from Takeuchi's TAK triple-recursion (1978).
spheres.source: McCarthy ~1968-70 (devised); Manna & Pnueli, J.ACM 17(3):555-569, 1970 + Manna & McCarthy, Machine Intelligence 5, 1970 (first proofs); Manna 1974 (popularized); Takeuchi 1978 (TAK, separate); Knuth 1991 (generalized a,b,c,d)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new, and arguably the BEST-fitting classic for the I-13 surface - no arrays, no strings, no state. The whole function is a single named recursive procedure f64 -> f64: def m(n){ if n>100 {->n-10} -> m(m(n+11)) }. Every value it ever touches (91, 100, 101, 111, and any input in range) is an exact integer far inside f64's 2^53 exact-integer bound, so there is no rounding. Verified: m(1)=m(50)=m(99)=m(100)=m(101)=91 and m(111)=101. It exercises exactly what the 8/19 benchmark's RUNTIME GOVERNORS guard - recursion depth (bounded at 4096 frames) and totality; m_91 is the canonical 'does this obviously-tangled recursion even terminate?', and here it runs, bounded and total, in the counted language.
spheres.blurb: The McCarthy 91 function is m(n) = n-10 if n>100, else m(m(n+11)) - a double self-application whose control flow is almost impossible to trace by eye, yet it is total and returns exactly 91 for every n<=100 (and n-10 above). McCarthy built it as a deliberate trap for program verifiers: the whole difficulty is seeing that a nest of m(m(m(...))) collapses to one constant. Credit: McCarthy devised it (~1968-70); the '91' is its output, not a version number. Mis-dating to avoid: it does NOT come from Manna's 1974 book - it was introduced in two 1970 papers (Manna & Pnueli, J.ACM 17(3); Manna & McCarthy, Machine Intelligence 5), which give the first formal proofs; the book only popularized it. It is structurally Ackermann-like but BOUNDED - the challenge is termination and collapse, not explosive growth - and it is total over all integers (including negatives), distinct from Takeuchi's TAK (1978). In real I-13 it is nothing new and arguably the best-fitting classic: one def m(n) with a single comparison and the nested double call, every value an exact f64 integer (verified m(1)=m(50)=m(99)=m(100)=m(101)=91, m(111)=101). It exercises exactly what the benchmark's runtime governors guard - recursion depth (bounded 4096) and totality.

spheres.title: KOSARAJU-SHARIR SCC
spheres.credit: The two-pass transpose method for strongly-connected components: forward DFS pushing vertices on finish, then DFS the TRANSPOSE (edge-reversed) graph in decreasing finish order, each tree a component. Named for S. Rao Kosaraju's UNPUBLISHED 1978 note; first put in print by Micha Sharir (1981, 'A strong-connectivity algorithm and its applications in data flow analysis', Comput. Math. Appl. 7(1):67-72) - independently - hence the fair name Kosaraju-Sharir (fixed by Aho-Hopcroft-Ullman's 1983 textbook, which credits both). It is NOT the first SCC algorithm: Tarjan's ONE-pass SCC (1972, dart 079) predates Kosaraju's note by six years and Sharir's publication by nine; the two-pass version is the simplest to TEACH, not the earliest, and Dijkstra's path-based single pass (1976) is another one-pass lineage. Mis-dating to avoid: Sharir is 1981 not 1979 (the nearby 1979 belongs to Aspvall-Plass-Tarjan's 2-SAT, which merely USES SCCs), and Kosaraju is 1978 not 1981. Neither invented DFS (Tremaux, 19th c.). It wins on clarity, not speed - two passes do ~double the DFS work plus building the transpose.
spheres.source: Kosaraju 1978 (unpublished); Sharir, Comput. Math. Appl. 7(1):67-72, 1981; Aho-Hopcroft-Ullman 1983 (names both); Tarjan 1972 (one-pass, dart 079); Dijkstra 1976 (path-based); Tremaux 19th c. (DFS)
spheres.i13_recommend: the SCC PARTITION is LIT via mutual reachability. Encode the digraph as per-vertex successor bitmasks (adj=[2,4,9,16,8] for 0->1, 1->2, 2->{0,3}, 3->4, 4->3); transitive closure by OR-to-fixpoint gives each vertex's reach set; two vertices share an SCC iff MUTUALLY reachable, and counting the SCC-minimal vertices gives the count. Verified: reach(0)=31 (all five), reach(3)=24 ({3,4}), mutual(0,1)=1, mutual(0,3)=0, mutual(3,4)=1, SCC count = 2, components = [0,0,0,1,1] - the same partition Tarjan gets in one pass. The transpose is FREE (encode the digraph as two parallel edge arrays and swap their roles - 'reverse every edge' costs nothing). What runs is the SCC RESULT; Kosaraju's actual two-pass DFS (the efficient O(V+E) method the demo animates) wants a threaded visited-array + a finish stack - expressible by threading value-semantic arrays, the same pattern as the corpus's other graph darts (Tarjan 079, Dijkstra 055).
spheres.blurb: Kosaraju-Sharir finds strongly-connected components in two DFS passes: run a DFS over the whole digraph and push each vertex when it finishes; then reverse every edge to form the transpose (which has identical SCCs) and DFS it in decreasing finish order - each tree the second search grows is exactly one SCC. The whole correctness is one line: a and b are mutually reachable in a graph iff they are in its transpose. Credit: it is named for Kosaraju's unpublished 1978 note but was first printed by Sharir (1981), independently - hence Kosaraju-Sharir (Aho-Hopcroft-Ullman 1983 credited both). It is NOT first: Tarjan's one-pass SCC (1972, dart 079) predates it by six years, and Dijkstra's path-based single pass (1976) is another; two-pass is the simplest to teach, not the earliest, and not the fastest (it does ~double the DFS work plus builds the transpose). Mis-dating: Sharir is 1981 not 1979, Kosaraju is 1978 not 1981; neither invented DFS (Tremaux, 19th c.). In real I-13 the SCC partition is LIT via mutual reachability: per-vertex successor bitmasks, transitive closure by OR-to-fixpoint, and two vertices share an SCC iff mutually reachable (verified reach(0)=31, reach(3)=24, count 2, components [0,0,0,1,1] - the partition Tarjan gets in one pass). The transpose is free (swap two parallel edge arrays); the full two-pass DFS the demo animates wants a threaded visited-array + finish stack, the corpus's standing graph pattern.

spheres.title: THE ROBINSON UNIFICATION
spheres.credit: J. Alan Robinson, 'A Machine-Oriented Logic Based on the Resolution Principle', JACM 12(1):23-41, 1965 - coined 'unification' and 'most general unifier' and put it at the center of machine proof. But the IDEA is Jacques Herbrand's (1930 thesis: an algorithm for solving systems of first-order term equations, 35 years before the name). Robinson's 1965 algorithm is worst-case EXPONENTIAL in time and space (the MGU written as an explicit tree can be 2^n) - 'unification is linear' is true only on a shared DAG. Linear unification has TWO parents: Paterson & Wegman (JCSS 1978, truly O(n) on a DAG) and Martelli & Montanari (TOPLAS 1982, the transformation-rule form, near-linear with union-find) - do not merge them or mis-date M-M as 1976. The occurs-check is the part Prolog's default =/2 SKIPS for speed (unsound: it 'unifies' X with f(X)); ISO Prolog adds a separate unify_with_occurs_check/2.
spheres.source: Robinson, JACM 12(1):23-41, 1965; Herbrand 1930 (thesis); Paterson & Wegman, JCSS 16(2):158-167, 1978; Martelli & Montanari, ACM TOPLAS 4(2):258-282, 1982; Prolog (Colmerauer/Kowalski 1972-74, occurs-check omitted); Huet 1976 + Corbin-Bidoit 1983 (union-find DAG)
spheres.i13_recommend: the scoped unifier is LIT. A first-order term is a flat node array; variables are negative f64 codes, constants positive; the substitution is an f64 array indexed by variable id; resolve() dereferences a bound variable by recursion, and binding is a value-semantic array update. Verified: unify f(X,b) with f(a,Y) -> ok=1, MGU {X=101(a), Y=102(b)}; unify f(X,X) with f(a,b) -> ok=0 FAIL (X binds to a, then the second X must equal b but a != b - the consistency check). The FRONTIER is arbitrary nested terms - a general term is a tree of nodes (a node arena, PS-015) and the full occurs-check walks that tree; the demo animates the node-pool unifier including the occurs-check on X ~ f(X). It is the engine dart 135 (Hindley-Milner) runs on.
spheres.blurb: Unification asks whether two terms containing variables - say f(X,b) and f(a,Y) - can be made literally identical by a single substitution, and if so returns the MOST GENERAL one: {X to a, Y to b}, committing to exactly what the terms force and no more. Robinson's method walks the two in lockstep: same function symbol and arity, recurse on argument pairs; a variable meets a term, bind it after the OCCURS-CHECK (the variable must not appear inside the term, or you would build an infinite term); two different constants fail. It is the hidden engine under Prolog resolution, Hindley-Milner type inference (dart 135), term rewriting, and theorem proving. Credit: J. Alan Robinson (1965) coined 'unification' and 'most general unifier', but the idea is Herbrand's (1930); Robinson's own algorithm is worst-case EXPONENTIAL (linear unification is Paterson-Wegman 1978 on a DAG and Martelli-Montanari 1982 with union-find); and the occurs-check is what Prolog's default =/2 skips for speed, unsoundly. 'Most general' is technical: the MGU is the least element (up to renaming) in the lattice of unifiers. In real I-13 the scoped unifier is LIT: terms as flat tagged f64 arrays (vars negative, consts positive), the substitution as a threaded f64 array, resolve() by recursion (verified f(X,b)~f(a,Y) -> X=a,Y=b; f(X,X)~f(a,b) -> FAIL); the frontier is arbitrary nested terms (a node arena, PS-015).

spheres.title: HINDLEY-MILNER TYPE INFERENCE
spheres.credit: Three distinct results with three dates, from people who never collaborated: J. Roger Hindley (1969, 'The Principal Type-Scheme of an Object in Combinatory Logic', Trans. AMS 146) proved the principal-type theorem for COMBINATORY LOGIC; Robin Milner (1978, 'A Theory of Type Polymorphism in Programming', JCSS 17:348-375) independently gave Algorithm W for ML and added LET-POLYMORPHISM; Luis Damas & Milner (1982, POPL) proved W sound AND complete (the correctness proof 'Hindley-Milner' silently drops). Algorithm W is 1978, not 1982. James Morris discovered type inference independently in 1968 (a year before Hindley) and is almost always omitted. Algorithm W is the SPECIFICATION you prove correct, not the shipping code - real ML/OCaml/Haskell compilers use union-find (Milner's Algorithm J) with Remy's level-based generalization. 'HM is exponential so it's impractical' misreads the 1990 DEXPTIME-completeness result (Kfoury-Tiuryn-Urzyczyn; Mairson): the worst case needs deeply nested lets; ordinary programs infer in near-linear time.
spheres.source: Hindley, Trans. AMS 146:29-60, 1969; Milner, JCSS 17:348-375, 1978 (Algorithm W); Damas & Milner, POPL 1982 (soundness+completeness); Robinson 1965 (unification, dart 134); Morris 1968 (independent); Remy 1988 (levels); Kfoury-Tiuryn-Urzyczyn / Mairson 1990 (DEXPTIME)
spheres.i13_recommend: the inference core is LIT, on the same engine as dart 134. Type variables are f64 ids; a bound variable used twice forces the SAME id, so lambda x. x is a -> a (verified: param var == body var); the K combinator lambda x. lambda y. x is a -> b -> a (the outer param is reused in the body, b never constrained - verified via var reuse); an application f x mints a fresh result variable and UNIFIES the type of f with (type of x -> result) - and unifying a fresh (unbound) variable with an arrow simply binds it (verified ok=1, the fresh var becomes the arrow), which is exactly the rule that types f x. The FRONTIER is full nested type terms + let-generalization: a type is a tree (node arena, PS-015), and generalization quantifies free variables. The demo animates the whole Algorithm-W inference of lambda f. lambda x. f x -> (a -> b) -> a -> b; the compiler grounds the fresh-var + unify core.
spheres.blurb: Hindley-Milner infers the MOST GENERAL type of a program with no annotations at all: give every unknown a fresh type variable, and at every application unify (dart 134) the function's type with (argument -> result); what survives is the PRINCIPAL type, proven to exist and be unique. lambda x. x gets a -> a; lambda f. lambda x. f x gets (a -> b) -> a -> b. Credit is three results with three dates: Hindley (1969) proved the principal-type theorem for combinatory logic; Milner (1978) gave Algorithm W for ML and added let-polymorphism; Damas & Milner (1982) proved W sound AND complete (the part the hyphenated name drops). They never collaborated, and Algorithm W is 1978 not 1982. Real compilers run Milner's union-find Algorithm J, not W; and the 1990 DEXPTIME-completeness result is about deeply nested lets, not ordinary code (which infers near-linearly). In real I-13 the inference core is LIT on the dart-134 engine: type variables are f64 ids, a variable used twice forces the same id (lambda x.x -> a->a, verified), and an application unifies a fresh var with an arrow, which binds (verified ok=1); the frontier is full nested type terms + generalization (a node arena, PS-015). The demo animates the full inference of (a->b)->a->b.

spheres.title: LIVE-VARIABLE ANALYSIS
spheres.credit: Gary Kildall's 'A Unified Approach to Global Program Optimization' (POPL 1973, pp. 194-206) gave the FRAMEWORK - facts form a lattice, transfer functions are monotone, iterate to a fixpoint - he did NOT invent dataflow analysis. Round-robin flow analysis was already flagging possibly-uninitialized variables in a Fortran compiler c.1961-63 (Vyssotsky & Wegner, Bell Labs), and Allen & Cocke had global dataflow at IBM (1969-71). Kildall's own four worked applications span FORWARD problems (constant propagation, CSE, redundant register loads) AND a BACKWARD one - live-variable analysis, which he performs by reversing the graph edges with an empty exit boundary. So liveness is one of his own examples; what he did NOT invent is dataflow analysis itself. It JOINS with UNION from bottom (a variable is live if used on SOME path before redefinition - do not copy the intersection/must template of available-expressions), the boundary sits at the EXIT (live_out[exit] = empty), and a loop's back edge is exactly why one pass is insufficient. Iterating gives the MFP (maximal fixed point), which equals the ideal meet-over-all-paths only for DISTRIBUTIVE frameworks (Kam-Ullman 1977).
spheres.source: Kildall, POPL 1973, pp. 194-206; Vyssotsky & Wegner c.1961-63 (Bell Labs); Allen & Cocke 1969-71 (IBM); Kam & Ullman, JACM 23(1) 1976 + Acta Informatica 7 1977 (monotone frameworks); Aho-Sethi-Ullman (Dragon Book) canonical statement; feeds Chaitin register allocation (dart 137)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - a variable set is one f64 bitmask; use and def are per-block masks; the transfer function live_in = use | (live_out - def) is bit-OR with bit-and-not (x - (x & def)); a block's live_out is the bit-OR of its successors' live_in; the backward sweep iterates to a fixpoint by recursion. Verified on a 4-block program (vars a=1, b=2, c=4): live_in = [ {}=0, {a}=1, {a,b}=3, {c}=4 ]. It is the input to register allocation (dart 137): two variables INTERFERE exactly when both are live at some point, which builds the interference graph colored next. A general CFG's successor structure is a graph (adjacency), the corpus's standing shape.
spheres.blurb: A variable is LIVE at a point if its current value may still be read before it is overwritten. Live-variable analysis is the classic BACKWARD, MAY dataflow: live_in = use UNION (live_out MINUS def), live_out = UNION over successors of live_in, iterated to a fixpoint (it joins with union from bottom; the boundary sits at the EXIT, not the entry; a loop's back edge is why one pass is not enough). It is the analysis that draws the interference graph for register allocation (dart 137): two variables interfere iff both are live at once. Credit: Gary Kildall (POPL 1973) gave the lattice-and-fixpoint FRAMEWORK, not the idea - round-robin flow analysis caught uninitialized variables at Bell Labs c.1961-63 (Vyssotsky-Wegner), and Allen & Cocke had global dataflow at IBM; Kildall's own four applications include liveness (backward, by edge reversal) alongside the forward ones - what predates him is dataflow analysis itself. Iterating gives the MFP, equal to the ideal meet-over-all-paths only for distributive frameworks (Kam-Ullman 1977). In real I-13 it is nothing new: a variable set is one f64 bitmask, the transfer use | (out - def) is bit-or and and-not, successor union is bit-or, and the backward sweep iterates to a fixpoint by recursion (verified live_in = [{}, {a}, {a,b}, {c}] = [0,1,3,4]). It feeds the interference graph colored in dart 137.

spheres.title: GRAPH-COLORING REGISTER ALLOCATION
spheres.credit: Chaitin et al. ('Register allocation via coloring', Computer Languages 6:47-57, 1981; the sole-author 'Yorktown allocator' adding spilling, 1982) built the FIRST working graph-coloring allocator, inside IBM's PL.8 compiler for the 801 RISC. But the reduction of register allocation to vertex-coloring is A. P. Ershov (1962, USSR); Cocke & Schwartz floated it at IBM/NYU c.1971 without implementing it. The 'simplify' step (delete a vertex of degree < k, color the rest, color it last) is Kempe's degree-reduction lemma from 1879 - straight out of his (flawed, Heawood 1890) four-color proof. Chaitin proved register allocation NP-complete (every graph is some program's interference graph), but that is only the GENERAL case: strict-SSA-form interference graphs are CHORDAL, colorable optimally in linear time (Hack; Bouchez; Pereira-Palsberg, 2005-07). Chaitin's coloring is a greedy heuristic that spills PESSIMISTICALLY on the spot; Briggs-Cooper-Torczon (1994) OPTIMISTIC coloring pushes the candidate and re-checks at select, where a color has often freed up.
spheres.source: Chaitin et al. 1981 (Computer Languages 6:47-57) + Chaitin 1982 (SIGPLAN, spilling); Kempe 1879 (Amer. J. Math. 2, degree-reduction / four-color); Ershov 1962 (USSR); Briggs-Cooper-Torczon, TOPLAS 16(3), 1994 (optimistic); chordal-SSA result 2005-07; consumes liveness (dart 136)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the interference graph is per-node adjacency bitmasks; coloring scans each node's neighbours into a USED-COLOR mask and takes the lowest color < k; if none is free, the node is marked spilled. Verified: K4 on {0,1,2,3} at k=3 registers -> colors [0,1,2] and node 3 SPILLS (its neighbours use all three colors), spills=1 (a K4 needs 4 colors > k=3, so a spill is unavoidable no ordering can dodge); a triangle {0,1,2} at k=3 -> colors [0,1,2], spills=0. Kempe's simplify is a degree test, all f64 + bitwise. It CONSUMES liveness (dart 136): the interference edges come from 'live at the same time'. A dense interference graph is an adjacency matrix (PS-004); the corpus flattens it to per-node masks, exact up to 63 nodes.
spheres.blurb: Graph-coloring register allocation models machine registers as COLORS: build the interference graph (two variables live at the same time interfere), then k-color it where k is the number of registers; whatever cannot be colored is SPILLED to memory. The clique number is a hard floor: a K4 needs 4 colors, so with k=3 a spill is unavoidable no matter the ordering. The method is simplify (Kempe: remove a node of degree < k, push it, color it last) then select (pop, give the lowest color no neighbour uses; spill if none). Credit: Chaitin et al. (1981-82, IBM PL.8) built the first working allocator, but the reduction is Ershov's (1962) and simplify is Kempe's (1879, from the four-color proof); and 'register allocation is NP-complete' is only the general case - strict-SSA interference graphs are chordal, colorable in linear time. Chaitin spills pessimistically; Briggs et al. (1994) optimistic coloring often does better. In real I-13 it is nothing new: the interference graph is adjacency bitmasks, coloring scans neighbours to a used-color mask and takes the lowest color < k, else spills (verified K4 at k=3 -> colors 0,1,2 + one spill; triangle -> 0 spills). It consumes liveness (dart 136); a dense interference matrix is PS-004, flattened to per-node masks.

spheres.title: THE DOMINATOR TREE
spheres.credit: Node d DOMINATES node n if every path from entry to n passes through d; the immediate dominator idom(n) is the closest strict dominator, and the idom edges form the dominator tree. Lengauer & Tarjan (TOPLAS 1(1):121-141, 1979) made computing it FAST, not first: dominance is Reese Prosser's (1959, via a Boolean connectivity matrix - but he gave no algorithm to compute it), and the first actual algorithm is Lowry & Medlock's (CACM 1969, a fixpoint, already shipping in an IBM OS/360 compiler a decade earlier). Lengauer-Tarjan is NEAR-linear (O(m alpha(m,n)) with inverse Ackermann), not truly linear; genuine linear time came 20 years later (Alstrup, Harel, Lauridsen & Thorup, 1999). The well-engineered simple ITERATIVE method storing only an idom[] array (Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy, 2001) often beats Lengauer-Tarjan in practice. SSA form is Rosen-Wegman-Zadeck (1988); the dominance-frontier phi-placement is Cytron-Ferrante-Rosen-Wegman-Zadeck (1991) - two layers, not one.
spheres.source: Lengauer & Tarjan, TOPLAS 1(1):121-141, 1979; Prosser 1959 (dominance concept); Lowry & Medlock, CACM 12(1):13-22, 1969 (first algorithm); Alstrup-Harel-Lauridsen-Thorup 1999 (linear); Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy 2001 (simple iterative idom[]); Cytron et al. 1991 (dominance frontiers / SSA)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - each Dom(n) set is one f64 bitmask; the update Dom(n) = {n} UNION (INTERSECT over predecessors p of Dom(p)) is bit-OR of (1<<n) with the bit-AND of the predecessors, iterated to a fixpoint. Verified on a diamond CFG (0->1, 0->2, 1->3, 2->3, 3->4): Dom(0)={0}=1, Dom(1)={0,1}=3, Dom(2)={0,2}=5, Dom(3)={0,3}=9, Dom(4)={0,3,4}=25; immediate dominators idom(3)=0 and idom(4)=3 - the merge point 3 is dominated only by 0, NOT by either branch 1 or 2, which is the whole point. A CFG is a graph (adjacency), the corpus's standing shape; dominance is the substrate SSA and its phi-placement stand on - the same lowering the 8/19 benchmark grades.
spheres.blurb: Node d dominates node n if every path from entry to n passes through d; the immediate dominator idom(n) is the closest strict dominator, and the idom edges form the DOMINATOR TREE - what must run before control can reach each block. It is the backbone of SSA form (phi-placement by dominance frontiers) and most modern optimization. Compute it by intersection to a fixpoint: Dom(entry)={entry}, Dom(n) = {n} UNION (intersection of predecessors' Dom sets). Credit: Lengauer & Tarjan (1979) made it FAST, not first - dominance is Prosser's (1959, no algorithm), the first algorithm is Lowry-Medlock's (1969, already shipping); Lengauer-Tarjan is near-linear (inverse Ackermann), true linear is Alstrup et al. (1999), and the simple iterative idom[] method (Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy 2001) often wins in practice. SSA is Rosen-Wegman-Zadeck (1988); phi-placement by dominance frontiers is Cytron et al. (1991). In real I-13 it is nothing new: each Dom set is a bitmask, the update {n} UNION intersect-of-preds is bit-or and bit-and, iterated to a fixpoint (verified diamond CFG: Dom(3)={0,3}, Dom(4)={0,3,4}; idom(3)=0, idom(4)=3 - the merge 3 escapes both branch dominators).

spheres.title: MARK-AND-SWEEP GC
spheres.credit: John McCarthy invented garbage collection for Lisp on the IBM 704 (implemented 1959, published April 1960, 'Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions', CACM 3(4)) and coined the term - the original MARK-SWEEP: mark everything reachable from the roots, then sweep the heap freeing the unmarked. But the pointer-reversal that runs the mark phase with a mark bit + a direction bit per cell and NO auxiliary stack is Schorr & Waite (CACM 1967), discovered independently by L. Peter Deutsch (~1965) - hence 'Deutsch-Schorr-Waite', not McCarthy. Reference counting (George Collins, CACM Dec 1960) is a DIFFERENT family (count incoming pointers, not trace reachability) - not first, not tracing, and it LEAKS cyclic garbage that mark-sweep reclaims. Mark-sweep does NOT move, compact, or copy - it flips bits and relinks free cells, leaving the heap fragmented (compaction/copying is a separate lineage: Minsky 1963, Fenichel-Yochelson 1969, dart 140). Classic mark-sweep is strictly STOP-THE-WORLD; incremental/concurrent tri-color GC is Dijkstra et al. 1978 (dart 141).
spheres.source: McCarthy, CACM 3(4), 1960 (invented GC / mark-sweep); Collins, CACM 3(12), Dec 1960 (reference counting, separate family); Schorr & Waite, CACM 10(8), 1967 (pointer reversal) + Deutsch ~1965; Knuth TAOCP Vol.1 1968; separate copying/incremental lineage darts 140/141
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - each object's children are a successor bitmask; MARK is a DFS from the roots that ORs each reached object into a 'marked' mask (recursion guarded by the already-marked bit); SWEEP is the bitwise complement within the heap. Verified: roots {0}, edges 0->{1,2}, 1->{3}, plus a garbage CYCLE 4->5->6->4; survivors = {0,1,2,3} = mask 15, freed = 127 - 15 = 112 = {4,5,6}. The garbage cycle 4->5->6->4 is COLLECTED - the exact case reference counting leaks forever. Reachability-from-the-root is the corpus's own shape: every inhabitant FOLDS TO ROOT_0, and here what folds to a root SURVIVES. A real heap of pointer objects is a node arena (PS-015); the corpus runs the reachability on adjacency masks.
spheres.blurb: Mark-and-sweep is the first garbage collector and the plainest statement of what 'alive' means: MARK every object reachable from the roots (a graph traversal), then SWEEP the whole heap and free everything left dark. Reachability IS survival. Its one real win over reference counting: it reclaims CYCLIC garbage - a ring of objects pointing at each other but at nothing the program can still see. Credit: John McCarthy (1959-60) invented GC for Lisp and coined the term, but the pointer-reversal that marks with no stack is Schorr-Waite's (1967, and Deutsch independently); reference counting (Collins, Dec 1960) is a different family, not first, and it leaks cycles; compaction/copying is a separate lineage (dart 140). Classic mark-sweep is strictly stop-the-world and leaves the heap fragmented - it flips bits, it does not move objects. In real I-13 it is nothing new: each object's children are a successor bitmask, MARK is a DFS from the roots ORing reached objects into a marked mask, SWEEP is one bitwise complement (verified survivors {0,1,2,3}=15, freed {4,5,6}=112 - a garbage cycle refcounting would leak). Reachability-from-the-root is the corpus's own shape: what folds to ROOT_0 survives.

spheres.title: CHENEY COPYING GC
spheres.credit: C. J. Cheney, 'A Nonrecursive List Compacting Algorithm', CACM 13(11):677-678, November 1970 - two pages - removed the recursion STACK from copying GC: the to-space itself becomes the breadth-first work queue, swept by a SCAN pointer chasing a FREE pointer, forwarding each child. But Cheney did NOT invent copying garbage collection: the copy-and-compact idea is Minsky's (MIT AI Memo 58, 1963, copying live cells out to disk and back), and the first IN-CORE two-semispace copier with forwarding pointers is Fenichel & Yochelson's (CACM Nov 1969) - but recursive. So forwarding pointers and semispaces are not Cheney's either; what he removed is the stack. 'Uses no extra space' is overstated: no auxiliary STACK, but a copying collector still needs a whole second semispace standing empty (~2x address space). Baker (1978) makes it incremental/real-time (a read barrier); Ungar's generation scavenging (1984) runs a Cheney copier over the young generation only; Moon (1984) named the cost - BFS order scatters a record's children across pages, wrecking locality.
spheres.source: Cheney, CACM 13(11):677-678, 1970; Minsky, MIT AI Memo 58, 1963 (first copying, via disk); Fenichel & Yochelson, CACM 12(11), 1969 (first in-core semispace, recursive); Baker, CACM 21(4), 1978 (incremental); Ungar 1984 (generation scavenging); Moon 1984 (locality cost)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - to-space is an f64 array used as a queue; SCAN and FREE are two integer indices; a 'forwarding pointer' is a visited-bit plus the copy position. Copy each root into to-space; then walk from scan to free, and for each copied object enqueue its not-yet-forwarded children (advancing free) or reuse the forward. Verified: roots {0}, edges 0->{1,2}, 1->{3}, garbage {4,5}; 4 live objects copied in BFS order [0,1,2,3], scan meets free at 4 -> done, and the garbage {4,5} is NEVER scanned or copied. No recursion stack - the queue IS the to-space, exactly Cheney's trick. Pairs with mark-sweep (dart 139): both trace reachability from roots, but Cheney COMPACTS (copies live, forwards, leaves gaps behind) where mark-sweep frees in place. A real heap wants a node arena (PS-015); the corpus runs the BFS + forwarding on arrays.
spheres.blurb: Cheney's copying collector traverses live objects with NO recursion and NO auxiliary stack: copy each root into to-space leaving a FORWARDING pointer in from-space, then scan the copied objects breadth-first using two pointers - SCAN (next to process) and FREE (next empty slot) - so the growing to-space IS the work queue. It compacts (no fragmentation) and touches only live data. Credit: C. J. Cheney (1970, two pages) removed the recursion STACK, but did not invent copying GC - that is Minsky (1963, via disk) and Fenichel-Yochelson (1969, the first in-core semispace with forwarding pointers, but recursive). 'No extra space' is overstated: no auxiliary stack, but a whole second semispace stands empty (~2x address space). Baker (1978) made it incremental; Ungar's generation scavenging (1984) runs it over the young generation; Moon (1984) named the cost - BFS order wrecks locality. In real I-13 it is nothing new: to-space is an f64 array used as a queue, scan and free are two indices, forwarding is a visited-bit + copy position (verified 4 live objects copied in BFS order [0,1,2,3], garbage {4,5} never touched). The queue IS the to-space, exactly Cheney's trick; pairs with mark-sweep (139) as trace-vs-compact.

spheres.title: TRI-COLOR MARKING
spheres.credit: WHITE = not yet reached (candidate garbage), GRAY = reached but children not scanned, BLACK = reached and fully scanned; the INVARIANT is 'no black object points directly to a white one', and maintaining it (with write barriers) lets the collector run interleaved with the mutating program. The white/gray/black formulation, the strong invariant, and its proof are Dijkstra, Lamport, Martin, Scholten & Steffens (CACM 21(11):966-975, 1978) - FIVE authors, not just Dijkstra (circulated as EWD 630, 1977). And concurrent GC was published earlier by Guy Steele (CACM 1975, semaphores + marking, three years before, though NOT the color scheme); Dijkstra's EWD 492 (1975) posed the problem. Ben-Ari (1984) gave a much simpler proof (effectively two colors). Barrier mis-attribution is the most common error: the snapshot-at-the-beginning / DELETION barrier is Yuasa (1990, shade the OLD referent), NOT Dijkstra, whose is an INSERTION barrier (shade the NEW referent). The named 'tricolour abstraction' vocabulary is Wilson's (1992). Every production concurrent collector (Go, Java G1/ZGC/Shenandoah, .NET) is this 1978 invariant plus a choice of barrier.
spheres.source: Dijkstra, Lamport, Martin, Scholten & Steffens, CACM 21(11):966-975, 1978 (EWD 630, 1977); Steele, CACM 1975 (first concurrent GC); Ben-Ari, TOPLAS 6(3), 1984 (simpler proof); Yuasa 1990 (deletion barrier); Wilson 1992 ('tricolour abstraction'); McCarthy 1960 (two-color mark-sweep, dart 139)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - color is an f64 array (0 white / 1 gray / 2 black); the sweep finds a gray node, greys its white children (value-semantic array update), blackens it, and recurses to a fixpoint; a final pass checks that no black object has a white child. Verified: root {0}, edges 0->1->2 reachable, garbage 3->4 plus isolated 5; final black (live) = {0,1,2} = 7, white (garbage) = {3,4,5} = 56, gray = {} at fixpoint, and the invariant 'no black -> white' has 0 violations (HOLDS). The tri-color INVARIANT is the corpus's kind of law - a property preserved through every step. It completes the GC triad with mark-sweep (139, stop-the-world two-color) and Cheney (140, copying): tri-color is what makes marking INCREMENTAL. A real concurrent heap needs write barriers on a node arena (PS-015); the corpus grounds the marking + the invariant on a color array.
spheres.blurb: Tri-color marking is the white/gray/black abstraction that lets a garbage collector run WHILE the program is still running. White = not yet reached (candidate garbage); gray = reached but children not scanned; black = reached and fully scanned. The INVARIANT - no black object points directly to a white one - is what makes it safe to pause and resume the collector interleaved with the mutator (maintained by write barriers). Roots start gray; repeatedly take a gray object, paint its white children gray, and paint it black; when no gray remains, every white object is garbage. Credit: the white/gray/black formulation and the strong invariant are Dijkstra, Lamport, Martin, Scholten & Steffens (CACM 1978) - FIVE authors, not just Dijkstra - and concurrent GC was Steele's first (1975, though not the colors). The snapshot/DELETION barrier is Yuasa (1990), NOT Dijkstra (whose is an INSERTION barrier); the name 'tricolour abstraction' is Wilson's (1992). Every production concurrent collector (Go, Java G1/ZGC/Shenandoah, .NET) is this 1978 invariant plus a barrier. In real I-13 it is nothing new: color is an f64 array (0/1/2), the sweep greys white children and blackens gray nodes to a fixpoint, and one pass checks the invariant (verified black {0,1,2}, garbage {3,4,5}, 0 violations). It completes the GC triad with mark-sweep (139) and Cheney (140); the invariant is the corpus's kind of preserved-through-every-step law.

spheres.title: THE SECD MACHINE
spheres.credit: Peter Landin, 'The Mechanical Evaluation of Expressions', Computer Journal 6(4):308-320, 1964 - the FIRST abstract machine for evaluating lambda / applicative expressions, and the paper that COINED the closure (a lambda body paired with the environment relative to which it is evaluated). Corrections: the C in SECD is CONTROL, not Code (it holds the expressions still to be evaluated; compiled-SECD work like Henderson's LispKit, 1980, later loads compiled code); SECD is CALL-BY-VALUE, not lazy (the argument 3+1 becomes 4 BEFORE the body is entered - the call-by-name dual is Krivine's, dart 143); Landin did not conjure lexical scope from nothing (ALGOL 60 block structure predates him) but he did formalize the closure as a machine value fixing McCarthy's 1960 dynamic-scope FUNARG bug; ISWIM ('The Next 700 Programming Languages') is a SEPARATE 1966 paper. Plotkin (1975) gave the first formal verification, pinning SECD as call-by-value; the dump D is a stack of saved (S,E,C) states = a reified continuation, which is exactly why Felleisen & Friedman (1986) could delete it for the CEK machine.
spheres.source: Landin, Computer Journal 6(4):308-320, 1964; McCarthy 1960 (env, dynamic scope); Plotkin, TCS 1(2):125-159, 1975 (call-by-value verification); Henderson 1980 (LispKit SECD instruction set); Felleisen & Friedman 1986 (CEK, deletes the dump); Danvy 2004 (SECD = CPS defunctionalized)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - S is an f64 array with a top pointer, E is an environment array, C is a control array of opcodes, and a closure is a first-order record (a body index + an environment). Because Landin's machine is already FIRST-ORDER (closures are data, dispatch is explicit), it ports to a closureless language directly. Verified evaluating ((\x. x+x) (3+1)): the argument 3+1 is evaluated to 4 FIRST (call-by-value), then the body x+x reads x twice from E and sums to 8 on the stack. Landin's machine is a DEFUNCTIONALIZED evaluator (dart 147), which is precisely why a language with NO closures can run it. A full lambda term + the dump of saved states wants a node arena (PS-015); the corpus runs the stack/env core on flat arrays. It is the direct ancestor of the CEK machine and every bytecode VM - including the 8/19 benchmark's Cortex VM.
spheres.blurb: The SECD machine (Landin, 1964) is the first abstract machine for the lambda calculus: it evaluates an expression by rewriting a four-register state - Stack of computed values, Environment of variable bindings, Control of what is still to do, Dump of saved caller states. A lambda pushes a CLOSURE (its body paired with the captured environment) - the concept Landin coined - and it is CALL-BY-VALUE: arguments are fully evaluated before the call. Corrections: the C is Control, not Code; SECD is call-by-value not lazy (in ((\x.x+x)(3+1)) the 3+1 becomes 4 before the body runs - the call-by-name dual is Krivine, dart 143); it was the first ABSTRACT machine (four registers, prose rewrite rules), with the concrete instruction set coming later (Henderson's LispKit, 1980); and ISWIM is a separate 1966 paper. Plotkin (1975) verified it as call-by-value; the dump is a reified continuation, which is why Felleisen (1986) deleted it for the CEK machine. In real I-13 it is nothing new: S/E/C are arrays with pointers and a closure is a first-order record, so Landin's already-defunctionalized machine ports to a closureless language directly (verified ((\x.x+x)(3+1)): 3+1=4 by value, then x+x = 8). It is the ancestor of every bytecode VM, including the 8/19 benchmark's Cortex VM.
spheres.kicker: dart 142 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE KRIVINE MACHINE
spheres.credit: Jean-Louis Krivine designed the minimal call-by-name abstract machine in the EARLY 1980s; it circulated unpublished for ~25 years and was formally published only in 2007 ('A call-by-name lambda-calculus machine', Higher-Order and Symbolic Computation 20(3):199-207) - so it is NOT a 2007 invention. It is the call-by-NAME DUAL of Landin's SECD (1964), not its descendant: SECD is call-by-value with a four-register state including a dump; SECD's actual heir is the CEK machine. Corrections: call-by-name is NOT lazy - a discarded argument is never evaluated (the good part), but an argument used twice is RE-evaluated each time because the bare machine has no sharing; laziness (call-by-need) adds sharing, which is Sestoft's update markers (1997) and the graph-reduction idea (dart 145). de Bruijn indices (nameless variables, the count of binders to the use's own binder) are de Bruijn's (1972), a decade earlier - the machine merely READS them in its Access rule. The named opcodes ACCESS/GRAB/PUSH are the compiled-machine presentation (Curien's tradition); the bare machine reaches only WEAK HEAD normal form (full normal form needs Cregut 1990).
spheres.source: Krivine, HOSC 20(3):199-207, 2007 (designed early 1980s); Landin 1964 (SECD, the CBV dual); de Bruijn 1972 (nameless indices); Sestoft, JFP 7(3), 1997 (call-by-need via update markers); Ager-Biernacki-Danvy-Midtgaard 2003 (derive it by CPS + defunctionalization)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the term is a flat tagged f64 array, the argument stack and environment are arrays with top pointers, and the three moves (Push an argument / Grab it into a lambda / Access a variable) are index arithmetic. Krivine's closures are first-order DATA records (a de Bruijn index + an environment index), not host-language function values, which is exactly why it ports to a closureless language. Verified on (\x.\y. x) 42 (expensive), where expensive = sum 1..20: call-by-name returns 42 and forces the discarded argument 0 steps (y is never demanded), while call-by-value returns 42 but wastes 20 steps evaluating the argument before discarding it. The bare machine reaches weak head normal form; adding SHARING (call-by-need) is Sestoft's update markers - and sharing is exactly what graph reduction (dart 145) provides. Full lambda terms want a node arena (PS-015).
spheres.blurb: The Krivine machine is the smallest machine that actually runs the lambda calculus: a term, an environment, an argument stack, and three moves - Push an argument, Grab it into a lambda, Access a variable. It is CALL-BY-NAME, so a function's argument is only evaluated if and when the body demands it: an argument that is thrown away is never evaluated. And its closures are first-order DATA records (a de Bruijn index + an environment index), not host-language function values, which is exactly why it ports to a first-order language. Credit: Krivine designed it in the EARLY 1980s (published only in 2007) - not a 2007 invention; it is the call-by-name DUAL of SECD, not its descendant (SECD's heir is CEK). Corrections: call-by-name is not lazy (a discarded arg is skipped, but an arg used twice is re-evaluated - laziness adds sharing, Sestoft 1997); de Bruijn indices are de Bruijn's (1972), merely read by the Access rule; and the bare machine reaches only weak head normal form. In real I-13 it is nothing new: the term is a flat tagged array, the stack/env are arrays with pointers, and the closureless machine ports directly (verified (\x.\y.x) 42 (expensive): both give 42, but call-by-name wastes 0 steps on the discarded argument while call-by-value wastes 20). It is the call-by-name counterpart to SECD (142); sharing is what graph reduction (145) adds.
spheres.kicker: dart 143 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: SKI COMBINATOR CALCULUS
spheres.credit: Moses Schonfinkel introduced combinators in a 7 December 1920 Gottingen talk ('Elemente der Logik') and the 1924 paper 'Uber die Bausteine der mathematischen Logik' (Math. Annalen 92:305-316), expressly to ELIMINATE bound variables - this is the true origin. Haskell Curry INDEPENDENTLY rediscovered them in late 1927 at Princeton (unaware of the 1924 paper), coined the theory of combinatory logic (1930 thesis) and the modern letters B, C, K, W - so 'Curry invented combinators' is wrong. Corrections: Schonfinkel's own letters were S, C, I, Z, T (his C, Konstanzfunktion, is the modern K); 'currying' is a misnomer - functions-of-one-argument-returning-functions is Schonfinkel's (1920) and traces to Frege (1893), and the NAME is Strachey's (1967), not Curry's own. You do not need all three combinators: I = S K K, and Schonfinkel himself showed S and K (his C) suffice; a single-combinator basis (Iota) is Fokker/Barker (1992/2001), NOT Schonfinkel's U. David Turner did NOT invent SKI or combinator reduction (1920s); his 1979 contribution is ENGINEERING - compile a lazy functional language to SK combinators and run it by graph reduction (dart 145). S duplicates its third argument (S x y z -> x z (y z)), so terms can grow without bound and diverge - which is exactly why SKI is Turing-complete.
spheres.source: Schonfinkel 1920 (talk) / Math. Annalen 92:305-316, 1924; Curry 1927-30 (independent, combinatory logic); Frege 1893 (currying idea); Church 1936 / Turing 1937 (SKI is Turing-complete); Church-Rosser 1936 (confluence / unique normal form); Curry & Feys 1958 (bracket abstraction); Turner, SP&E 9:31-49, 1979 (compile lazy language to SK, graph reduction)
spheres.i13_recommend: the reduction rules are LIT. S, K, I are tag-dispatched reducers over an argument stack; a combinator with enough arguments fires its rule; there is NO environment because there are no variables to bind. Verified: I 7 = 7, K 7 99 = 7, and S K K 7 = (K 7)(K 7) = 7 = I 7, so S K K = I with NO variables anywhere. This is the corpus's COMPUTED-NOT-STORED axis in its purest form: identity is computed by reduction, never a stored name. A general term is a graph of applications (a node arena, PS-015) reduced by graph reduction (dart 145); the corpus grounds the reduction rules on the saturated redex. Combinators are how Turner ran a real functional language with no variables at all - the same closureless fit as defunctionalization (dart 147) and SECD (dart 142).
spheres.blurb: SKI combinator calculus: three constants - S, K, I - and two rewrite rules turn any lambda program into a tree of applications with NO bound variables. Rules: I x = x; K x y = x; S x y z = x z (y z). That is Turing-complete: every computable function is a fixed tree of S/K/I, and I is redundant (I = S K K), so two combinators suffice. Credit: Moses Schonfinkel introduced combinators in a 1920 Gottingen talk (1924 paper) to eliminate bound variables - the true origin; Curry independently rediscovered them (1927) and built the theory. Corrections: Schonfinkel's letters were S, C, I, Z, T (his C = the modern K); 'currying' is a misnomer traced to Frege (1893), named by Strachey (1967); a single-combinator basis (Iota) is Fokker/Barker (1992/2001) not Schonfinkel's U; and Turner (1979) did not invent SKI - he compiled a lazy language to it and ran it by graph reduction. S duplicates its argument, which is why SKI can diverge and is Turing-complete. In real I-13 the reduction rules are LIT: S/K/I are tag-dispatched reducers over an argument stack, with NO environment because there are no variables (verified I 7=7, K 7 99=7, S K K 7 = 7 = I 7, so S K K = I). This is the computed-not-stored axis in its purest form - identity computed by reduction, never a stored name; a general term wants a node arena (PS-015) reduced by graph reduction (145).
spheres.kicker: dart 144 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: GRAPH REDUCTION
spheres.credit: Christopher Wadsworth INVENTED graph reduction in his 1971 Oxford D.Phil thesis ('Semantics and Pragmatics of the Lambda-Calculus'): represent the term as a graph (DAG) so identical subterms are ONE shared node, reduced at most once via in-place update. David Turner did NOT invent it - his 1979 contribution ('A New Implementation Technique for Applicative Languages', SP&E 9:31-49) is COMBINATOR (variable-free) graph reduction, standing on Wadsworth's sharing and Schonfinkel/Curry's combinators (dart 144). Corrections: graph reduction is a MECHANISM (sharing + in-place update), while lazy/call-by-need evaluation is a STRATEGY (evaluate only when needed, and only once) - they are named and crystallized separately by Henderson & Morris and Friedman & Wise (both 1976). String reduction (Berkling 1975) is NOT graph reduction done linearly: it COPIES a shared subterm and re-reduces every copy, exactly the inefficiency graph reduction avoids by keeping one DAG node. The G-machine (Johnsson & Augustsson 1984) COMPILES the graph instead of interpreting it; the Spineless Tagless G-machine (Peyton Jones 1992, GHC) went 'tagless' - but GHC REINTRODUCED pointer tags in 2007 after measuring branch mispredictions on modern CPUs.
spheres.source: Wadsworth 1971 (Oxford thesis, invented graph reduction); Turner, SP&E 9:31-49, 1979 (combinator graph reduction); Henderson-Morris + Friedman-Wise 1976 (lazy evaluation named); Berkling 1975 (string reduction, copies); Johnsson-Augustsson 1984 (G-machine); Peyton Jones 1992 (STG); Marlow et al. 2007 (pointer tagging)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - a reduction that returns [value, count] threads the work count; the TREE form evaluates 2+3 twice (2 additions), the GRAPH form binds the shared node once and reuses it (1 addition) - same result 25 (verified). The sharing IS the value-semantic let binding: bind the sub-result once, use it twice. A real reduction graph is a node arena with in-place update (PS-015) - and I-13's value-semantic array update is the immutable form of exactly that (cf. the persistent segment tree, dart 124). It provides the sharing that turns the closureless combinators (dart 144) into a fast lazy language, and adds to the Krivine machine (dart 143) the one thing call-by-name lacks: sharing, i.e. call-by-need.
spheres.blurb: Graph reduction writes the program as a GRAPH, not a tree: identical subexpressions become one shared node, reduced at most once and updated in place. That single trick - sharing plus in-place update - is the mechanism under every lazy functional language: let sq = 2+3 in sq*sq computes 2+3 a single time, where a tree would compute it twice. Credit: Christopher Wadsworth invented it (1971 Oxford thesis) - NOT Turner, whose 1979 contribution is COMBINATOR (variable-free) graph reduction standing on it. Corrections: graph reduction is a mechanism, lazy evaluation (Henderson-Morris / Friedman-Wise, 1976) is the strategy; string reduction (Berkling) copies-and-re-reduces, the opposite of keeping one DAG node; the G-machine (1984) compiles the graph, and GHC's Spineless Tagless G-machine went tagless but re-added tags in 2007 after measuring branch mispredicts. In real I-13 it is nothing new: a reduction returning [value, count] threads the work count, and the tree form does 2 additions where the graph form binds the shared node once (1 addition) - same result 25 (verified). The sharing IS the value-semantic let binding; a real reduction graph is a node arena with in-place update (PS-015), whose immutable form is I-13's value-semantic array update (cf. the persistent segment tree, dart 124). It gives the combinators (144) their speed and the Krivine machine (143) its sharing (call-by-need).
spheres.kicker: dart 145 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE FUTAMURA PROJECTIONS
spheres.credit: Yoshihiko Futamura STATED the three projections in 1971 ('Partial Evaluation of Computation Process - An Approach to a Compiler-Compiler', Trans. IECE Japan 54-C(8):721-728) - specialize an interpreter to a fixed program = compiled program (1st); specialize the specializer to the interpreter = compiler (2nd); specialize the specializer to itself = compiler-generator (3rd) - but he did NOT implement them. No self-applicable partial evaluator existed until the Copenhagen DIKU group's mix in 1984-85 (Jones, Sestoft & Sondergaard; full account 1989), a 14-year gap; binding-time analysis is what made self-application actually work. Corrections: 'mixed computation' is Andrei Ershov's coinage (1977-78, USSR, independent), NOT Futamura's; the DIKU group named their self-applicable partial evaluator 'mix' after Ershov's term; the existence of a specializer is Kleene's s-m-n theorem (1938/1952), but the s-m-n construction just staples the fixed input on and ADDS overhead, whereas partial evaluation OPTIMIZES; partial evaluation did not begin in 1971 (Lombardi & Raphael's incremental LISP, 1964; the practical Linkoping REDFUN, 1976, both predate the first self-applicable system); self-application is NOT required to get a compiler (you can write the cogen by hand: Holst-Launchbury; Birkedal-Welinder); and specialization does not always speed things up (over-unrolling bloats code).
spheres.source: Futamura, Trans. IECE Japan 54-C(8):721-728, 1971; Kleene s-m-n (1938/1952); Ershov 1977-78 (mixed computation; the DIKU 'mix' tool is named after it); Jones-Sestoft-Sondergaard 1984-85 / 1989 (first self-applicable mix); Jones-Gomard-Sestoft 1993 (the textbook); PyPy meta-tracing / Truffle-Graal (modern)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the generic power(base, exp, acc, mults) recurses over the exponent, threading a multiply-count; the SPECIALIZED pow3(base) = base*base*base has NO exponent parameter and NO loop test. Verified: generic power(2,3) = 8 in 3 multiplies (with a loop test each step); specialized pow3(5) = 125 in 2 multiplies (0 loop tests). The specialization IS Futamura's 1st projection: interpreter + fixed program (exp=3) = compiled program. It is the corpus's own shape at the meta-level - the campaign grounds each dart by SPECIALIZING a general algorithm to one concrete input and running it. Full self-applicable mix wants a program representation to specialize (a term/AST arena, PS-015).
spheres.blurb: The Futamura projections are partial evaluation folded on itself. Specialize an interpreter to one fixed source program and you get that program compiled (1st projection); specialize the specializer to the interpreter and you get a compiler (2nd); specialize the specializer to itself and you get a compiler-generator (3rd) - one operation, partial evaluation, applied three times. Credit: Futamura (1971) STATED the projections but did not implement them; the first self-applicable partial evaluator (mix) is the Copenhagen DIKU group's (1984-85), a 14-year gap. Corrections: 'mixed computation' is Ershov's coinage (1977, independent), not Futamura's, and the DIKU group named their tool 'mix' after it; the s-m-n theorem (Kleene, 1938/1952) proves a specializer EXISTS but adds overhead, whereas partial evaluation optimizes; partial evaluation predates 1971 (Lombardi & Raphael 1964; REDFUN 1976); self-application is not required (write the cogen by hand); and specialization does not always speed things up (over-unrolling bloats code). In real I-13 it is nothing new: a generic power(base, exp) recurses over the exponent (threading a multiply-count), while specialized pow3(base) = base*base*base has no exponent param and no loop (verified generic 2^3=8 in 3 mults; pow3(5)=125 in 2 mults). That specialization IS the 1st projection: interpreter + fixed program = compiled program - the campaign's own meta-shape (each dart grounds by specializing a general algorithm to one input).
spheres.kicker: dart 146 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: DEFUNCTIONALIZATION
spheres.credit: John Reynolds COINED defunctionalization in 'Definitional Interpreters for Higher-Order Programming Languages' (Proc. 25th ACM Conf., 1972) - a whole program has only finitely many lambdas, so tag each with an integer, replace each first-class function value with a plain data record (the tag + its captured variables), and replace every call with ONE first-order apply(tag, arg) that switches on the tag. The term then lay largely UNUSED for a generation until Danvy & Nielsen revived it ('Defunctionalization at Work', PPDP 2001). Corrections: defunctionalization is NOT closure conversion - closure conversion keeps functions FIRST-CLASS (a closure becomes a code-pointer + environment, called INDIRECTLY through the pointer), whereas defunctionalization is FIRST-ORDER (a tag + a switch, no indirect call). Reynolds did not invent 'functions as data' - Landin's SECD closure (1964) already represented a function value as a data structure and McCarthy's eval/apply (1960) already had a global apply. The clean derivation of the SECD/CEK/Krivine machines by 'CPS-transform then defunctionalize the continuations' is Ager-Biernacki-Danvy-Midtgaard (2003), not the 1972 paper. Defunctionalization CAN be typed: Pottier & Gauthier (2004) show it is type-preserving precisely when the tag/apply type is a GADT. The inverse, refunctionalization, is Danvy (2006), only a LEFT inverse.
spheres.source: Reynolds 1972 ('Definitional Interpreters', coins the term); Danvy & Nielsen, PPDP 2001 (revive it); Landin 1964 (closure as data) + McCarthy 1960 (global apply); Ager-Biernacki-Danvy-Midtgaard 2003 (machine derivation); Pottier & Gauthier, POPL 2004 (typed, GADTs); Danvy-Millikin 2006-09 (refunctionalization)
spheres.i13_recommend: the technique is LIT and load-bearing. A 'function value' is an integer tag, and apply(tag, x) is an if-chain that dispatches. Verified: apply(0,5) = 15 (tag 0 = n+10), apply(1,5) = 10 (tag 1 = n*2), and map over [1,2,3] with tag 0 -> [11,12,13] - a higher-order map running with NO closures. Because I-13 has no first-class functions, this is exactly how every higher-order pattern (map, fold, callbacks) is expressed on the corpus - Reynolds's 1972 transformation is the corpus's native idiom. It is the deep tie of the whole batch: SECD (142), Krivine (143), SKI (144), and CPS (149) all become runnable on a closureless language precisely by DEFUNCTIONALIZING their higher-order parts (the closure, the continuation). Captured free variables want a record (PS-015); here the lambdas are closed, so a bare tag suffices.
spheres.blurb: Defunctionalization (Reynolds, 1972): a whole program has only finitely many lambdas, so tag each with an integer, replace every first-class function value with a plain data record (the tag + its captured variables), and replace every call with one first-order apply(tag, arg) that switches on the tag - higher-order functions vanish. It is the exact transformation a language with NO first-class functions needs. Credit: Reynolds coined it (1972), then it lay unused for a generation until Danvy & Nielsen revived it (2001). Corrections: it is NOT closure conversion (which keeps functions first-class via a code-pointer + environment, called indirectly) - defunctionalization is first-order (a tag + a switch); Reynolds did not invent functions-as-data (Landin's closure, 1964; McCarthy's apply, 1960); the machine-derivation use ('CPS then defunctionalize the continuation') is Ager-Biernacki-Danvy-Midtgaard (2003); and it CAN be typed (Pottier & Gauthier 2004, via GADTs). In real I-13 the technique is LIT and load-bearing: a function value is an integer tag and apply(tag, x) is an if-chain (verified apply(0,5)=15, apply(1,5)=10, map over [1,2,3] with tag 0 -> [11,12,13], with no closures). Because I-13 has no first-class functions, this is how every higher-order pattern is expressed on the corpus - and it is the deep tie of the batch, since SECD (142), Krivine (143), SKI (144), and CPS (149) all run on a closureless language by defunctionalizing their higher-order parts.
spheres.kicker: dart 147 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THREADED CODE
spheres.credit: James Bell gave the first PUBLISHED definition, name, and four-step dispatch analysis in 'Threaded Code' (CACM 16(6):370-372, 1973, received June 1971) - but he did NOT invent it: his own paper thanks the team behind DEC's PDP-11 FORTRAN IV compiler, which ALREADY generated threaded code, and Charles Moore had built (indirect) threaded code into the first Forth at NRAO around 1970, independently and contemporaneously (Bell's paper was still in submission). Subroutine-threaded code (a bare list of CALLs) is the honest assembly-folklore predecessor with no single inventor. Corrections: Dewar (CACM 18(6), 1975) PUBLISHED and named INDIRECT threaded code and proved it more compact than Bell's direct form, but Moore had been running indirect threading in Forth ~5 years earlier; 'computed-goto / direct threading is always ~2x faster than a switch' was true on the superscalar CPUs Ertl & Gregg measured (2001-03) but Rohou-Swamy-Seznec (CGO 2015) showed modern ITTAGE branch predictors erase much of the gap - 'don't trust folklore'; and 'threaded' has NOTHING to do with multithreading/concurrency - the thread is a single strand of control woven through a fixed set of primitives, a data structure.
spheres.source: Bell, CACM 16(6):370-372, 1973 (first published, received June 1971); Charles Moore ~1970 (Forth, indirect threading); Dewar, CACM 18(6):330-331, 1975 (indirect threaded, named); GCC labels-as-values + CPython 3.1 2009 (computed-goto); Rohou-Swamy-Seznec, CGO 2015 (don't trust folklore)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the program is an f64 opcode array; the operand stack is an array with a top pointer; the dispatch loop is a recursion that reads prog[pc] and branches on the opcode. Verified on [PUSH 2, PUSH 3, ADD, PUSH 4, MUL, HALT]: PUSH grows the stack, ADD/MUL pop two and push one, and it computes (2+3)*4 = 20. This is a DEFUNCTIONALIZED interpreter (dart 147): opcodes are tags, the switch is the apply. It is literally what the 8/19 benchmark's Cortex WASM VM does at its core - the AST-to-IVM lowering produces a bytecode that a dispatch loop runs. The full VM (branches, calls) wants more opcodes but the same array + pointer machinery; direct-threading / computed-goto is a dispatch OPTIMIZATION, not a new model.
spheres.blurb: In threaded code the compiled program is just a list of addresses (or opcodes) of primitive routines, run by a tiny dispatch loop: fetch the next token, jump to its routine, which does its work and returns to the loop. It is Forth's inner interpreter and the beating heart of every bytecode VM - the 'thread' is the single strand of control woven through a fixed set of primitives (nothing to do with concurrency). Credit: James Bell (CACM 1973) gave the first published definition and name, but DEC's PDP-11 FORTRAN already generated threaded code and Charles Moore built it into Forth (~1970) independently; subroutine-threading is the assembly-folklore predecessor. Corrections: indirect threading is Dewar (1975, published; Moore ran it earlier); the folklore 'computed-goto is always ~2x faster' is false on modern branch predictors (Rohou et al. 2015); and 'threaded' is unrelated to multithreading. In real I-13 it is nothing new: the program is an f64 opcode array, the operand stack is an array with a top pointer, and the dispatch loop is a recursion branching on the opcode (verified [PUSH 2, PUSH 3, ADD, PUSH 4, MUL, HALT] -> (2+3)*4 = 20). It is a defunctionalized interpreter (dart 147) - opcodes are tags, the switch is the apply - and literally what the 8/19 benchmark's Cortex WASM VM runs at its core.
spheres.kicker: dart 148 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: CONTINUATION-PASSING STYLE
spheres.credit: Continuation-passing style gives every function one extra argument - a CONTINUATION representing 'the rest of the computation' - so nothing ever returns: each operation calls its continuation with its result, and control flow becomes explicit data. Continuations have MANY independent discoverers, famously catalogued by Reynolds ('The Discoveries of Continuations', 1993): Adriaan van Wijngaarden gave the earliest known CPS transform (Sept 1964, IFIP Working Conference), and Landin's SECD DUMP (1964) is already a reified continuation. The CPS transform proper is Michael Fischer (1972, 'Lambda calculus schemata'); Gordon Plotkin (1975) proved the call-by-value / CPS simulation theorem; Guy Steele's 'Lambda: The Ultimate Declarative' (1976, the concept) and the RABBIT Scheme compiler (1978 master's thesis) used CPS as a compiler INTERMEDIATE FORM so tail calls become jumps - the lineage behind SSA and modern IRs. So do not credit CPS to one inventor: the discovery is genuinely plural (van Wijngaarden, Mazurkiewicz, F. L. Morris, Fischer, the SECD dump).
spheres.source: Reynolds 1993 ('The Discoveries of Continuations'); van Wijngaarden 1964 (earliest CPS transform); Landin 1964 (SECD dump = reified continuation); Fischer 1972 (CPS transform); Plotkin 1975 (CBV/CPS simulation); Steele 1976 ('Lambda: The Ultimate Declarative') + RABBIT 1978 (CPS as compiler IR)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - a continuation is a stack of pending [op, arg] frames in an f64 array; each operation computes its value and INVOKEs the continuation (a recursion that pops the next frame), so 'the rest of the computation' is data. Verified evaluating (2+3)*4: add(2,3) -> 5, invoke the continuation [MUL 4] -> 5*4 = 20, invoke [HALT] -> 20, with control explicit and nothing using a native return. Because I-13 has no closures, the continuation is DEFUNCTIONALIZED (dart 147) into that stack - which is precisely the SECD DUMP (dart 142) and the CEK machine's K. This closes the batch's loop: SECD's dump, Krivine's stack, and CPS's continuation are the SAME object (a reified continuation), all runnable on a closureless language by defunctionalization. First-class call/cc wants to capture the whole stack as a value (a saved-state arena, PS-015).
spheres.blurb: In continuation-passing style, every function takes one extra argument - a CONTINUATION representing 'the rest of the computation' - and nothing ever returns: each operation calls its continuation with its result. Control flow (returns, calls, jumps) stops being hidden machinery and becomes data you pass around. It is the compiler intermediate form (Steele's RABBIT) and the way to make call/cc, exceptions, and generators explicit. Credit: continuations have MANY independent discoverers (Reynolds catalogued them: van Wijngaarden 1964, Mazurkiewicz, F. L. Morris, Fischer, the SECD dump) - do not credit CPS to one inventor. The CPS transform proper is Fischer (1972); the call-by-value simulation theorem is Plotkin (1975); CPS as a compiler IR is Steele ('Lambda: The Ultimate Declarative' 1976; the RABBIT compiler 1978), the lineage behind SSA. In real I-13 it is nothing new: a continuation is a stack of pending [op, arg] frames in an f64 array, and each operation invokes the continuation (a recursion popping the next frame), so the rest of the computation is data (verified (2+3)*4 = 20 with control explicit, no native return). Because I-13 has no closures, the continuation is defunctionalized (dart 147) into that stack - which is precisely the SECD dump (142) and the CEK machine's K. This closes the batch's loop: SECD's dump, Krivine's stack, and CPS's continuation are the same reified-continuation object, all runnable on a closureless language by defunctionalization.

spheres.title: THE 6502 GATE
spheres.kicker: a fold - EMULATION opens; the oracle before the CPU
spheres.credit: David Lee Wise / ROOT0 / TriPod LLC. The 2026-08-19 'i13 nes build v0' drop (rev2/rev5/rev7/rev8-0819): a 6502 CPU built oracle-first, graded against SingleStepTests/65x02 (a real chip dumped to 10,000 cases per opcode with per-cycle bus traces - NOT the author's). spheres.blurb: On 2026-08-19 the corpus opened a new interest - EMULATION - and renamed its language: I-13 is now compIle 13, because that is what an AI is, a compiler who can talk back (the capital I spells the 13). The first fold builds an NES / 6502 CPU the corpus way: the oracle before the CPU. A real chip's behaviour was dumped into 10,000 test cases per opcode with per-cycle bus traces (SingleStepTests / 65x02), and the gate feeds a candidate CPU those cases and reports the first place it disagrees with the real chip - 'a CPU with no oracle is a guess with a green tick.' Run this session: opcode $69 ADC passes 10,000/10,000 on state and again with per-cycle bus grading, and a planted wrong-overflow rule is caught in 2,500 cases (25%) - because a wrong overflow flag looks correct on three inputs of four, exactly why hand-written fixtures keep failing. Then 33 opcodes were written in compIle 13 itself and graded 33,000 times by that outside oracle: pass 1 (850/900) forced out an SBC overflow bug (the subtract-overflow rule was handed the inverted operand); pass 2 (6600/6600, 100%) fixed it to the original operand and killed a state-packing hack that could not survive a full 56-bit register file in a 53-bit double; pass 3 re-ran all 33 through a STRICT reader (33000/33000) that refuses exactly the seven P0 targets of the I-13 benchmark (a function that never returns, one-branch returns, duplicate names, a nested function, and more) - the strict reader IS the benchmark's conformance gate, and nothing had been leaning on the weaker one (luck, not judgement). The finding worth keeping is an oracle blind spot: inclusive-OR sets its zero flag only when both inputs are zero, which occurs in 0 of 10,000 cases, so deleting the flag entirely still scores 10000/10000 - proven by planting and by hand. 100% against an exhaustive suite is not 100% coverage. LIT: the gate ran, the two-reader divergence, the blind spot. AMBER: the kernel is not yet compiled (a model proved 12/12 faithful to the binary). OPEN: nothing touches an address yet, so nothing has met mirroring - the one failure mode this architecture is otherwise built to remove.
